Too Much of a Good Thing? Rethinking Choice Overload It has become something of a commonplace that modern consumers are overwhelmed by choice. Supermarkets stock tens of thousands of products, streaming services offer more films than anyone could watch in a lifetime, and even a cup of coffee can involve a bewildering series of decisions. Many commentators have argued that this abundance, far from making us happier, leaves us anxious and dissatisfied; some have even spoken of a 'tyranny of choice'. The idea has an intuitive appeal, but the scientific evidence behind it turns out to be more complicated than its popularity suggests. Much of the enthusiasm for the idea can be traced to a single experiment published in 2000 by the psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper. In an upmarket grocery store in California, they set up a tasting booth that displayed either 24 varieties of jam or just 6. The larger display attracted more shoppers: around 60 per cent of passers-by stopped at it, compared with 40 per cent for the smaller one. Yet when it came to buying, the pattern reversed. About 30 per cent of those who visited the small display went on to buy a jar, whereas only 3 per cent of those who visited the large display did so. (Visitors to either display received a discount coupon, which allowed the researchers to count purchases at the checkout.) The researchers concluded that too many options could discourage people from choosing at all, a phenomenon that came to be known as 'choice overload'. The study was elegant and its message memorable, and it quickly spread far beyond academic psychology. Business consultants advised companies to reduce their product ranges, and popular books argued that the explosion of consumer choice was contributing to unhappiness. In my view, the speed with which the finding was accepted owed as much to its appeal as a story as to the strength of the evidence. A single study, however striking, conducted in one shop over a short period, is a slender foundation on which to build general advice for entire industries. Subsequent research confirmed the need for caution. Some later experiments reproduced the effect, but others found no effect, and a few found the opposite: that people were more likely to make a choice, and more satisfied with their choices, when they had more options. In 2010, a team led by Benjamin Scheibehenne combined the results of 50 experiments in a statistical analysis known as a meta-analysis. They found that the average effect of choice overload across all of these studies was virtually zero. This did not mean that the original finding was wrong, but it did suggest that choice overload was far from a universal law of human behaviour. Some researchers also pointed out that studies with dramatic results are more likely to be published than studies that find nothing, a problem known as publication bias, which may have made the effect seem more consistent than it really was. Why might the effect appear in some situations and not others? Later work has begun to identify the conditions under which large assortments become a burden. A meta-analysis published in 2015 by Alexander Chernev and colleagues concluded that choice overload is more likely when the decision is difficult, when options are hard to compare, when people do not have clear preferences, and when they are trying to minimise the effort they spend deciding. A wine expert facing a long list of wines may relish the variety; a novice confronted with the same list may simply give up or pick at random. The way options are presented matters too: grouping products into categories, for instance, appears to make large assortments easier to navigate. What, then, should we conclude? It would be a mistake, I believe, to swing from one extreme to the other and declare that choice is never a problem. Most of us have experienced the paralysis of scrolling endlessly through options without settling on anything. But the evidence suggests that the problem lies less in the number of options than in the circumstances in which we confront them. Rather than simply reducing choice, businesses and policymakers might do better to help people choose: by organising options clearly, by offering sensible default options, or by providing tools that make comparison easier. There is also a broader lesson here about how psychological findings travel. The jam study was not a bad study; its authors were careful in describing what they had found. The problem was the eagerness of others to extract a simple rule from a single result. As psychology has become more aware of the need to replicate findings before treating them as established, the story of choice overload offers a useful reminder that the most memorable results are not always the most reliable. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Your home town • Where is your home town? • What do you like most about it? • Has your home town changed much since you were a child? • Would you like to live there in the future? Why or why not? Topic: Weather • What kind of weather do you enjoy most? • Does the weather ever affect your mood? • What do people in your country usually do when it rains? • Would you prefer to live somewhere hotter or colder than where you live now? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a time when you learned something new outside school or work. You should say: • what you learned • how and where you learned it • who, if anyone, helped you • and explain how you felt about learning it. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Do you still use this skill today? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Learning outside formal education • Why do you think many adults decide to learn new skills? • Is it better to learn a practical skill from a teacher or from online videos? • Do you think older people find it harder to learn new things? Why? Education and technology • How has technology changed the way people learn? • Some people say that schools should focus more on practical life skills. Do you agree? • In the future, do you think people will need to keep retraining throughout their working lives? END OF TEST

Today most vertical farms are more modest, but the basic principles are the same: plants are grown indoors, usually without soil, with their roots in water containing dissolved nutrients, and with light supplied by energy-efficient LEDs. Growing plants under glass is of course nothing new, but traditional greenhouses rely on the sun, whereas a vertical farm replaces sunlight entirely and can therefore be built almost anywhere, from basements to old factories and shipping containers. READING PASSAGE 3 (Questions 27-40) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below. In Defence of Boredom Boredom has a bad reputation. We tend to treat it as an unpleasant state to be escaped as quickly as possible, and modern life offers endless means of escape: at the first hint of tedium in a queue or on a train, most of us reach for our phones. Yet in recent years a number of psychologists and philosophers have argued that boredom is not simply a nuisance but an emotion with a purpose. I am not convinced that boredom is the hidden blessing some popular writers now claim, but I do think it deserves a fairer hearing than it usually receives. Part of the difficulty is that boredom is surprisingly hard to define. People use the word to describe everything from mild restlessness to deep despair. In 2012, the psychologist John Eastwood and his colleagues proposed that boredom is best understood as the unpleasant experience of wanting to engage in satisfying activity but being unable to do so. This seems to me a genuinely useful definition, because it explains why boredom feels uncomfortable rather than merely neutral: it involves a frustrated desire, not just an absence of stimulation. Just how uncomfortable boredom can be was shown in a much-discussed series of studies published in 2014 by Timothy Wilson and his team at the University of Virginia. Participants were asked to sit alone in a bare room for between six and fifteen minutes, with nothing to do but think. Most found the experience unpleasant. In one version of the study, participants were given the option of pressing a button to give themselves a mild electric shock, which they had earlier said they would pay money to avoid. Twelve of the eighteen men and six of the twenty-four women chose to shock themselves at least once rather than simply sit with their thoughts. Why would evolution have equipped us with such an unpleasant feeling? One answer, developed by the philosopher Andreas Elpidorou among others, is that boredom works rather like pain or hunger. Pain tells us that something is damaging our body; hunger tells us that we need food. Boredom, on this view, tells us that our current situation is failing to engage us and that we should look for something different. Seen this way, boredom is not an enemy but a signal, and it can push people towards goals that are more meaningful to them. Some researchers have gone further and suggested that boredom can make people more creative. In one well-known experiment, the psychologists Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman asked one group of participants to spend fifteen minutes copying telephone numbers from a directory, a deliberately dull task, while a control group did nothing beforehand. Both groups were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The participants who had been bored first came up with more ideas. The result is intriguing, but it should be treated with caution: the studies involved small numbers of people, and later attempts to find similar effects have produced mixed results. It would also be a mistake to romanticise boredom. Researchers distinguish between boredom as a passing state, which everyone experiences, and boredom proneness, a lasting tendency to feel bored frequently. People who are highly prone to boredom are more likely to report problems such as overeating, gambling and poor performance at school or work. In jobs that require constant attention but offer little variety, such as monitoring screens, boredom can also lead to dangerous mistakes. What, then, of smartphones? It would be too simple to blame technology for every difficulty we have in tolerating boredom; people complained of tedium long before the invention of the telephone. But constant access to entertainment may prevent boredom from doing its job. If we silence the signal the moment it appears, we never discover where it might have led us. For this reason, I believe that children in particular benefit from some unstructured time in which they are left to find their own amusement, even if they complain about it at first. Boredom, in the end, is neither good nor bad in itself. Like other uncomfortable emotions, it carries information, and its value depends on how we respond to it. Why would evolution have equipped us with such an unpleasant feeling? One answer, developed by the philosopher Andreas Elpidorou among others, is that boredom works rather like pain or hunger. Pain tells us that something is damaging our body; hunger tells us that we need food. Boredom, on this view, tells us that our current situation is failing to engage us and that we should look for something different. Seen this way, boredom is not an enemy but a signal, and it can push people towards goals that are more meaningful to them. Some researchers have gone further and suggested that boredom can make people more creative. In one well-known experiment, the psychologists Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman asked one group of participants to spend fifteen minutes copying telephone numbers from a directory, a deliberately dull task, while a control group did nothing beforehand. Both groups were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The participants who had been bored first came up with more ideas. The result is intriguing, but it should be treated with caution: the studies involved small numbers of people, and later attempts to find similar effects have produced mixed results. It would also be a mistake to romanticise boredom. Researchers distinguish between boredom as a passing state, which everyone experiences, and boredom proneness, a lasting tendency to feel bored frequently. People who are highly prone to boredom are more likely to report problems such as overeating, gambling and poor performance at school or work. In jobs that require constant attention but offer little variety, such as monitoring screens, boredom can also lead to dangerous mistakes. What, then, of smartphones? It would be too simple to blame technology for every difficulty we have in tolerating boredom; people complained of tedium long before the invention of the telephone. But constant access to entertainment may prevent boredom from doing its job. If we silence the signal the moment it appears, we never discover where it might have led us. For this reason, I believe that children in particular benefit from some unstructured time in which they are left to find their own amusement, even if they complain about it at first. Boredom, in the end, is neither good nor bad in itself. Like other uncomfortable emotions, it carries information, and its value depends on how we respond to it. The Language of the Hive A A honeybee that has found a rich patch of flowers faces a problem. The food is out in the landscape, perhaps several kilometres away, but the bees that could help collect it are in the dark interior of the hive. In the 1940s, the Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch announced a remarkable solution. Beekeepers had long noticed bees moving excitedly on the comb, but no one had understood the meaning of these movements. According to von Frisch, the returning forager performs a dance on the vertical surface of the honeycomb that tells her nestmates where the food is. Von Frisch spent decades refining his interpretation, and in 1973 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with two other pioneers of the study of animal behaviour. B The most informative movement is the 'waggle run'. The dancing bee moves forward in a straight line while vigorously shaking her abdomen from side to side, then circles back to her starting point and repeats the run, alternating between a right-hand and a left-hand return loop. The angle of the waggle run relative to the vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun: a run straight upwards means 'fly towards the sun', while a run pointing 40 degrees to the right of vertical means 'fly 40 degrees to the right of the sun'. The duration of the waggle run indicates distance; the longer it lasts, the further away the food. A single dance may contain dozens of waggle runs, and a particularly rich food source can keep a forager dancing for several minutes. C Remarkably, bees take account of the sun's movement across the sky. A forager that has been inside the hive for some time will adjust the angle of her dance to allow for how far the sun has moved since she was last outside. Bees can also determine the sun's position on cloudy days, as long as some patches of blue sky are visible, because they can detect patterns of polarised light that are invisible to humans. Experiments in which hives were moved to unfamiliar locations, or in which bees were shown artificial patterns of polarised light, have confirmed how flexible this navigational system is. Can We Trust What Witnesses Remember? For much of legal history, an eyewitness who confidently identified a suspect was regarded as among the most persuasive forms of evidence. Juries find such testimony compelling, and it is easy to see why: a person who saw a crime with their own eyes seems far more reliable than a chain of circumstantial clues. Yet over the past fifty years, psychological research has shown that human memory is far less like a video recording than most people assume. In my view, this research has rightly changed how courts treat eyewitness evidence, although some of the popular conclusions drawn from it go too far. Much of the early work was carried out by the American psychologist Elizabeth Loftus. In a classic study published in 1974, Loftus and John Palmer showed participants films of traffic accidents and then asked them how fast the cars had been going. The wording of the question mattered: participants asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other gave higher estimates of speed than those asked about cars that 'hit' each other. A week later, participants who had heard the word 'smashed' were also more likely to report having seen broken glass, even though there had been none in the film. Later studies went further, showing that it is possible to create memories of entire events that never happened. In one well-known experiment, a minority of adult participants, given false accounts said to come from their relatives, came to believe that as children they had been lost in a shopping centre. Findings like these led many people to conclude that memory is hopelessly unreliable. I think that conclusion is mistaken. What the research shows is that memory is reconstructive: each time we recall an event, we rebuild it from fragments, and the rebuilding can be influenced by what we have learned since. This makes memory vulnerable, but it does not make it worthless. The real-world consequences of memory errors have nonetheless been serious. Since the 1990s, DNA testing has led to the release of hundreds of people in the United States who had been wrongly convicted of serious crimes. According to the Innocence Project, an organisation that works on such cases, mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in roughly seven out of ten of these convictions. In most of these cases, the witnesses were not lying: they sincerely believed they were identifying the right person. One reason for these errors lies in the way identifications were traditionally obtained. In a typical line-up, a witness views a suspect alongside several other people and is asked whether the culprit is present. If the police officer running the line-up knows which person is the suspect, he or she may unintentionally signal this through words or body language. Witnesses who are told afterwards that they have chosen correctly tend to become more confident, and by the time a case reaches court, a hesitant initial choice may have become a certainty. This last point has led to a significant change in thinking about confidence. For many years, researchers argued that a witness's confidence was a poor guide to accuracy. More recent analyses, notably by the psychologists John Wixted and Gary Wells, suggest that the picture is more nuanced. Confidence expressed at the time of a witness's first identification, under fair conditions, can be a reasonably good indicator of accuracy; it is confidence that has grown later, through feedback and repetition, that is misleading. I find this argument convincing, and it has clear practical implications. Many police forces have now adopted reforms based on this research. Line-ups are increasingly run on a 'double-blind' basis, by an officer who does not know which person is the suspect. Witnesses are warned that the culprit may not be present, and their level of confidence is recorded immediately, in their own words, before they receive any feedback. These procedures do not eliminate error, but they make it much less likely that a witness's memory will be shaped by the investigation itself. Eyewitness testimony, then, should be neither blindly trusted nor automatically dismissed. Memory is a remarkable but imperfect system, and the task for the legal system is to collect and evaluate it in ways that respect both its strengths and its weaknesses. Working Less, Achieving More? The Four-Day Week The idea that people might one day work far fewer hours is not new. In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that within a century, rising productivity would allow his grandchildren's generation to work around fifteen hours a week. That prediction has not come true; in most wealthy countries, the standard working week has barely changed for decades. In recent years, however, a growing movement has argued for a four-day week without any loss of pay, and a series of trials has given the idea a credibility it previously lacked. I believe the evidence so far is genuinely encouraging, though it is not yet as conclusive as some campaigners suggest. The best-known trial took place in the United Kingdom in the second half of 2022. Sixty-one companies, employing around 2,900 people, agreed to reduce working time by about a fifth for six months, while paying staff the same. The organisations involved ranged from software firms and marketing agencies to a fish-and-chip shop. At the end of the trial, 56 of the 61 companies chose to continue with a shorter week, and 18 said that the change was permanent. Revenue, on average, stayed broadly the same, while employees reported less stress and burnout, better sleep and an easier balance between work and family life. Earlier, between 2015 and 2019, two large trials in Iceland had reduced the working week of more than 2,500 public-sector workers, from 40 hours to 35 or 36, again without any cut in pay. Researchers who analysed the results reported that productivity and service provision remained the same or improved in most workplaces, and the trials were followed by agreements that gave many Icelandic workers the right to shorter hours. These results are often cited, quite reasonably, as evidence that reduced hours can work in the public sector as well as in private business. How can people produce as much in four days as in five? Supporters offer several explanations. Long hours do not necessarily mean more output: tired workers make more mistakes, and much time in a typical office is lost to unnecessary meetings and distractions. When the working week is shortened, organisations are forced to look closely at how time is used. Many companies in the trials cut the length and number of meetings, introduced periods of uninterrupted work, and automated routine tasks. In this sense, the four-day week is less a gift of leisure than a demand for greater efficiency. There are, however, good reasons for caution. The companies that took part in the trials volunteered to do so, and they are likely to have been those most enthusiastic about the idea and most able to make it work. Their experience may not be typical of businesses in general. Moreover, six months is a short period; it is possible that the initial enthusiasm of managers and staff will fade, or that the pressure to fit five days' work into four will itself become a source of stress. Some employees in the trials did indeed report that their days had become more intense. The model also suits some jobs better than others. In office work, where tasks can often be reorganised, a shorter week may be achieved through greater efficiency. But in hospitals, schools, shops and factories, output depends heavily on the number of hours that staff are present. Reducing hours in these sectors without reducing pay would usually require hiring more people, which would increase costs. Some organisations have responded by offering a 'compressed' week, in which staff work the same number of hours over four longer days. In my view, this is not really a four-day week at all, and it may suit few employees with caring responsibilities. None of these difficulties is a reason to dismiss the idea. The trials so far suggest that, for many organisations, a shorter week can benefit employees without harming the business. What is needed now is longer and more varied research, including companies that have not volunteered, so that we can see which kinds of work benefit and which do not. Keynes's fifteen-hour week may remain a distant dream, but a four-day week for many workers no longer seems an unrealistic one. Whether it spreads will depend less on slogans than on careful evidence. Questions 27-30: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

In 2017, researchers even reported sleep-like behaviour in an upside-down jellyfish, an animal with no brain at all, only a loose network of nerve cells. To decide whether an animal is truly sleeping rather than simply resting, scientists look for several signs: the animal is less responsive to its surroundings, it usually adopts a particular posture, it can be woken quickly, and, crucially, if it is kept awake, it sleeps more later to make up for what it has lost. The jellyfish met all of these criteria. Their regular pulsing slowed at night, and they were slower to react when disturbed. B Some animals have found a remarkable way to sleep and stay alert at the same time. In dolphins and some seals, only one half of the brain sleeps at a time, while the other half remains awake. The eye connected to the waking half usually stays open, allowing the animal to watch for predators and, in the case of dolphins, to keep swimming and come to the surface to breathe. Many birds can do the same. In a well-known experiment, mallard ducks were placed in a row. The ducks at either end of the row slept with one eye open far more often than the ducks in the middle, and they kept open the eye that faced away from the group, towards possible danger. C The amount that animals sleep varies enormously. Some bats sleep for around twenty hours a day, waking mainly at dusk to feed. At the other extreme, giraffes in zoos sleep for less than five hours, often in very short naps. When researchers fitted wild African elephants with movement sensors, they found that the animals slept for only about two hours a night, mostly standing up, and sometimes went without sleep for nearly two days while moving long distances. Lost Without It? Satellite Navigation and the Human Sense of Direction Not long ago, finding your way around an unfamiliar city meant unfolding a paper map, working out where you were and planning a route. Today most people simply type a destination into a phone and follow the blue dot. Satellite navigation has made getting lost far less common, and it has undoubtedly saved travellers a great deal of time and stress. Yet a growing body of research suggests that this convenience may come at a price. When we hand the job of navigation to a machine, we may be giving up a skill that we are in danger of losing. To understand why, it helps to know how people normally find their way. Psychologists distinguish between two broad strategies. In the first, a person learns a sequence of actions: turn left at the bakery, go straight on past the church, take the second right. In the second, the person builds a mental map of the area, an understanding of where places are in relation to one another, which allows them to work out new routes and shortcuts. The second strategy is more flexible, and it depends heavily on a part of the brain called the hippocampus. Several studies have examined what happens to this system when people rely on navigation devices. In one experiment in Japan, researchers asked three groups of participants to walk to a series of destinations: one group used satellite navigation, another used a paper map, and a third had been shown the route in person beforehand. Those using satellite navigation walked further, stopped more often, and afterwards drew less accurate sketches of the area than either of the other groups. In another study, carried out in London, people's brain activity was recorded while they navigated a virtual version of a district of the city. Activity in the hippocampus increased when participants had to choose a route for themselves, but it largely disappeared when they were simply following instructions. These findings fit with what we know about the brain more generally. Like a muscle, the brain tends to strengthen the abilities that are used and to neglect those that are not. A study in Canada that followed a group of adults for three years found that those who used satellite navigation most heavily showed a steeper decline in spatial memory over that period. Importantly, the researchers found no evidence that people with a poor sense of direction were simply more likely to use the devices. This suggests, although it does not prove, that heavy use of navigation technology was itself responsible for some of the decline. It would be wrong to conclude from this that satellite navigation is harmful in itself or that we should abandon it. The technology has clear benefits, particularly for drivers, who are safer when they can concentrate on the road rather than on a map, and for people with conditions that make navigation genuinely difficult. In emergencies, it can be life-saving. In my view, the problem is not the technology but the way most of us use it: passively, without paying any attention to where we are going. There are simple ways to use satellite navigation more actively. Before setting off, travellers can look at the whole route on the map and note a few landmarks. During the journey, they can try to predict the next turn before the device announces it. Some researchers have proposed that devices themselves could be redesigned to encourage this, for example by showing nearby landmarks prominently or by giving directions in terms of the surroundings rather than distances. Children, in particular, should be given regular opportunities to find their way without a device, since the skills of navigation develop through practice in childhood. Some commentators argue that worrying about navigation skills is pointless, because machines will always be there to guide us. This seems to me too optimistic. Batteries die, signals fail in tunnels and remote areas, and devices sometimes give instructions that are plainly wrong. More importantly, the ability to form a mental map of the world is linked to the brain systems we use for memory more generally. Keeping those systems active may matter for reasons that go well beyond finding our way to the station. Questions 27-30: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Neighbours • Do you know your neighbours well? • How often do you talk to your neighbours? • Have you ever helped a neighbour? • What makes someone a good neighbour? Topic: Weekends • What do you usually do at the weekend? • Do you prefer busy or relaxing weekends? • How were your weekends different when you were a child? • Is there anything you would like to do at weekends but don't have time for? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a journey you remember well. You should say: • where you went • who you travelled with • how you travelled • and explain why you remember this journey so well. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Would you like to make the same journey again? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Travel • Why do some people prefer to travel on their own? • How has the way people go on holiday changed in recent years? • Do you think people learn more from travelling than from books? Journeys in the future • How might long-distance travel change in the next few decades? • Should governments discourage people from flying? • Will people still need to travel for work in the future, or will technology replace it? END OF TEST

The Puzzle of the Yawn A Few behaviours are as familiar, or as poorly understood, as the yawn. Almost all vertebrates yawn, including mammals, birds, reptiles and fish, which suggests that the behaviour is extremely old in evolutionary terms. Humans begin yawning before they are born: ultrasound scans have shown babies yawning in the womb from around the eleventh week of pregnancy. A typical yawn lasts about six seconds and follows a fixed sequence, a long, deep breath in with the jaw wide open, a brief pause at the peak, and a shorter breath out, and once it has started it is very difficult to stop. Yawning is not simply a sign of tiredness, either. People yawn most often shortly after waking and before going to sleep, but athletes, musicians and students often report yawning just before a race, a performance or an examination, when they are anxious and not at all sleepy. B The most common explanation offered for yawning is that it brings extra oxygen into the body, or removes excess carbon dioxide, when we are tired or bored. This idea was tested in the 1980s by the psychologist Robert Provine. He asked volunteers to breathe air containing different amounts of oxygen and carbon dioxide and recorded how often they yawned. Breathing air rich in carbon dioxide made people breathe faster, but it did not make them yawn more, and breathing pure oxygen did not make them yawn less. Provine concluded that yawning and breathing are controlled by separate mechanisms, and the oxygen theory has largely been abandoned by researchers, even though it remains popular with the general public. C A more recent theory, developed by the psychologist Andrew Gallup and his colleagues, proposes that yawning helps to cool the brain. The brain works best within a narrow range of temperatures, and the deep breath taken during a yawn, together with the stretching of the jaw, increases blood flow to the skull and brings in cooler air. In support of this idea, researchers have found that people yawned less often when they held a cold pack against their foreheads, or when they breathed through their noses, which cools the blood going to the brain, than when they held a warm pack or breathed through their mouths. D The cooling theory also makes a surprising prediction: people should yawn less when the air around them

Science for Everyone? The Rise of Citizen Science In 2007, a group of astronomers at the University of Oxford faced a problem. A telescope survey had produced images of around a million galaxies, and the researchers wanted to classify them according to their shape. Computers at the time could not do this reliably, and a single scientist working full-time would have needed years to look at them all. So the team launched a website called Galaxy Zoo, inviting members of the public to classify the galaxies themselves. Within a day of its launch, volunteers were classifying tens of thousands of galaxies an hour, and within a year more than a hundred thousand people had taken part. Each galaxy was classified many times by different people, and the combined results proved to be as accurate as those of professional astronomers. Galaxy Zoo is often described as the beginning of modern citizen science, but the idea of ordinary people contributing to research is much older. For more than a century, amateur birdwatchers in North America have taken part in an annual bird count, and their records now form one of the longest-running sources of information about changes in bird populations. Weather records kept by volunteers, observations of the first flowers of spring and amateur discoveries of comets have all made important contributions to science. What the internet has changed is the scale. Projects can now involve hundreds of thousands of people around the world, and smartphones allow volunteers to submit photographs, recordings and precise locations instantly. The benefits for scientists are obvious. Volunteers can collect data across areas far larger than any research team could cover, and they can process quantities of information that would otherwise be impossible to handle. In some cases, they have done more than simply provide labour. In 2011, players of an online puzzle game called Foldit, in which participants compete to fold protein molecules into their most stable shapes, worked out the structure of an enzyme from a virus related to HIV within three weeks, a problem that had defeated scientists for more than a decade. Volunteers have also made unexpected discoveries: one Galaxy Zoo participant, a Dutch schoolteacher, noticed an unusual glowing cloud of gas that turned out to be a previously unknown kind of astronomical object. There are also benefits for the volunteers and for society as a whole. People who take part in citizen science projects often say that they have learned a great deal, and some studies suggest that participation can increase people's understanding of how science works and their trust in scientific findings. In a period when scientific expertise is sometimes treated with suspicion, this seems to me one of the strongest arguments for encouraging such projects. Citizen science can also give local communities a voice: groups living near factories or busy roads have used their own measurements of air or water quality to persuade authorities to take action. Nevertheless, citizen science has its critics, and some of their concerns deserve to be taken seriously. The most common is that data collected by untrained volunteers may be unreliable. In practice, well-designed projects deal with this problem in several ways, for example by having each item checked by several people, by providing training and clear instructions, and by using statistical methods to identify unusual results. Studies comparing volunteer data with that of professionals have generally found that the quality is high, although it varies considerably between projects. A more difficult question concerns fairness. Volunteers give their time for free, and the results of their work are published in scientific journals, sometimes contributing to the careers of the professional scientists involved. Some projects now list volunteers as co-authors or thank them by name, but many do not. I believe that research institutions have a responsibility to recognise volunteers' contributions properly and to make the results of projects freely available to those who helped to produce them. If citizen science is seen simply as a source of free labour, it risks losing the goodwill on which it depends. Citizen science will not replace professional research, and nor should it. Many scientific questions require specialist knowledge, expensive equipment and years of training. But it has already shown that the public can be far more than passive consumers of science, and the number of projects is growing every year. Questions 27-30: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

Treasure on the Ocean Floor: The Debate over Deep-Sea Mining A Scattered across vast areas of the deep ocean floor, at depths of four to six kilometres, lie billions of dark, rounded lumps of rock about the size of a potato. These polymetallic nodules form extremely slowly, as metals dissolved in seawater build up in layers around a small object such as a shark's tooth or a fragment of shell, growing by just a few millimetres every million years. They are rich in manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper, metals that are used in large quantities in batteries, electric motors and electronic equipment. The largest known concentration lies in a region of the Pacific Ocean between Hawaii and Mexico, which covers several million square kilometres. Nodules are not the only mineral resource on the deep seabed. Metal-rich crusts form on the slopes of underwater mountains, and deposits of sulphide minerals build up around hot springs on the ocean floor, but nodules have attracted the most commercial interest because they can simply be collected from the surface of the sediment. B Most of the deep seabed lies beyond the control of any single nation. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the minerals in these areas are described as the 'common heritage of mankind', and mining there is regulated by the International Seabed Authority, an organisation based in Jamaica. The Authority has issued licences allowing companies and governments to explore for minerals, but it has not yet agreed on the rules that would allow commercial mining to begin, and negotiations over these rules have continued for many years. C Supporters of deep-sea mining argue that it is needed to meet the rapidly growing demand for metals used in clean-energy technologies. Mining on land, they point out, has serious environmental and social costs: forests are cleared, rivers are polluted, and in some countries mines have been associated with dangerous working conditions and child labour. READING PASSAGE 3 (Questions 27-40) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below. Pen or Keyboard? Why Handwriting Still Matters In many classrooms today, children spend more time typing than writing by hand, and the change has prompted a lively debate. Some educators argue that handwriting, and joined-up or cursive writing in particular, is an outdated skill that takes up valuable lesson time. In 2016, Finland removed the requirement to teach cursive writing from its national curriculum and placed greater emphasis on typing. Other countries have moved in the opposite direction: several American states that had dropped cursive from their schools have since passed laws to bring it back. Who is right? In my view, the evidence suggests that handwriting is far from obsolete, although not every form of it deserves the same priority. Much of the most interesting research concerns young children who are learning to read. In one series of studies, children who had not yet learned to read were taught letters in one of three ways: by writing them freehand, by tracing them, or by typing them on a keyboard. When the children were later shown letters while their brain activity was recorded, those who had learned by freehand writing showed much stronger activity in the brain regions used for reading than those in the other two groups. The researchers suggested that the messy, variable shapes produced by a child's own hand help the brain to learn what makes a letter recognisable. Similar arguments are made about older children. In a study carried out in the United States, children aged between about seven and twelve were asked to write essays both by hand and on a keyboard. The younger children in particular wrote more words, wrote faster and expressed more ideas when they used a pen than when they typed. The study was relatively small, however, and children who had been taught keyboard skills from an early age might have performed quite differently. Later research has produced mixed results, and I think it is wise to treat findings of this kind with some caution. Even so, there are good reasons to think that handwriting engages the brain in useful ways. For most adults, writing by hand is slower than typing, and this slowness forces the writer to select and organise information rather than simply recording it. A recent study that recorded brain activity in young adults found that writing by hand produced more widespread connections between different brain regions than typing did, a pattern associated with memory and learning. None of this proves that handwriting makes people cleverer, but it does suggest that the physical act of forming letters engages the brain in ways that pressing keys does not. There are also practical reasons for teaching handwriting. Many examinations are still taken on paper, and students whose handwriting is slow or difficult to read may be unable to show what they know. Children who struggle to form letters often find writing so tiring that they write less, which in turn limits the development of their written expression. For these children, early and regular practice can make a considerable difference. Handwriting also remains common in everyday life, from filling in forms to writing quick notes and cards, and some people find that planning their ideas on paper helps them to think more freely than working on a screen. The case for cursive writing is less clear. Supporters claim that joined-up writing is faster and helps with spelling, and that people who cannot read cursive will be unable to read historical documents or letters from older relatives. These arguments are not without merit, but the evidence that cursive offers special benefits over clear printed writing is limited. What matters most, it seems to me, is that children can write legibly and fluently, whatever style they use. None of this means that typing should be neglected. Most adults now do the majority of their writing on screens, and keyboard skills are essential for work and study. The sensible approach is not to choose between the pen and the keyboard but to teach both, giving handwriting priority in the early years, when it appears to support reading and spelling, and introducing typing as children grow older. Above all, decisions about the curriculum should be guided by evidence, rather than by nostalgia for the past or by enthusiasm for the latest technology. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Mornings • Are you a morning person? • What do you usually do first thing in the morning? • Has your morning routine changed since you were a child? • Do you prefer to study or work in the morning or in the evening? Topic: Sport • Do you play any sports? • What sports are popular in your country? • Did you do much sport at school? • Do you prefer watching sport or taking part? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe an occasion when you had to wait a long time for something. You should say: • what you were waiting for • how long you had to wait • what you did while you were waiting • and explain how you felt about the wait. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Are you generally a patient person? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Patience • Why do some people find it difficult to wait? • Do you think young people are less patient than older people? • In what situations is patience most important? The pace of modern life • Why does modern life seem to move so quickly nowadays? • What are the disadvantages of always wanting things immediately? • How could people slow down their lives? END OF TEST

B Although escalators have changed in appearance since then, the basic mechanism remains much the same. Each step is attached to a pair of chains that form a continuous loop, driven by an electric motor at the top. Wheels on each step run along two tracks, and the tracks are shaped so that the steps form a staircase on the incline but flatten out at the top and bottom, allowing passengers to step on and off safely. The steps then turn upside down and return underneath. A moving handrail, driven by the same motor, travels at the same speed as the steps, while metal plates with teeth like a comb, known as comb plates, guide each step into the landing so that nothing can be trapped. The Case for Learning by Heart For much of history, learning by heart was at the centre of education. Children recited multiplication tables, poems, lists of rivers and the dates of kings, and the ability to repeat long passages from memory was regarded as a sign of a well-educated mind. Over the last century, however, memorisation has fallen out of favour. It is now commonly dismissed as 'rote learning', a mechanical activity that produces parrots rather than thinkers, and many teachers have been encouraged to replace it with activities that develop understanding and creativity. I believe that this rejection has gone too far, and that a certain amount of learning by heart deserves a place in every classroom. The most common objection is that memorisation is pointless when any fact can be found in seconds on a phone. This argument, it seems to me, misunderstands how thinking works. Psychologists distinguish between working memory, which holds the small amount of information we are actively thinking about, and long-term memory, which stores what we know. Working memory is severely limited; most people can hold only a handful of new items in mind at once. When the facts we need are already secure in long-term memory, they can be called up without effort, leaving working memory free for reasoning. A pupil who must stop to work out seven times eight has little capacity left for the problem that the calculation was meant to solve. The point is illustrated by a well-known series of studies of chess players. When experienced players were shown a position from a real game for a few seconds, they could reconstruct it almost perfectly, while beginners remembered only a few pieces. When the pieces were placed randomly, however, the experts did little better than the beginners. Their advantage lay not in a superior memory in general but in a vast store of familiar patterns, built up over years, which allowed them to see meaning where a novice saw only a jumble. Expertise in any field, I would argue, rests on a similar foundation of stored knowledge. None of this is to defend the dreary drills that critics rightly remember from their own schooldays. Memorising words without understanding them is of little value, and pupils who can recite a definition but cannot apply it have learned very little. The aim should be to commit to memory material that has already been understood, or that will be understood more fully as a result of being remembered. A poem learned by heart, for example, can be turned over in the mind long after the lesson has ended, and its meanings may only become clear years later. Research on memory also suggests that the methods used in many schools are inefficient. Reading notes again and again, which many students consider the best way to revise, produces a feeling of familiarity but relatively poor long-term retention. Far more effective is what psychologists call retrieval practice: trying to recall information without looking at it, for instance by answering questions or testing oneself with cards. Spreading this practice out over days and weeks, rather than cramming it into a single evening, improves retention still further. It also helps to mix different topics within a single session, so that learners must work out which knowledge is relevant to each question. Learning by heart, done well, is therefore not a matter of endless repetition but of regular, effortful recall. There are also less obvious benefits. Pupils who have learned a speech or a poem by heart often speak with greater confidence, because they have a stock of well-made sentences to draw on. Some teachers report that memorisation can be a source of pride for pupils who struggle in other areas of school, since it rewards effort rather than prior advantage. These claims are harder to measure, and I would not want to overstate them, but they are consistent with my own experience as a teacher. I am not suggesting that schools should return to the classrooms of a hundred years ago. Discussion, investigation and creative work all have an essential role to play. But understanding and memory are not opposites; each depends on the other. A curriculum that ignores memory in the name of understanding risks producing pupils who have been taught to think but have nothing to think about. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Birthdays • How do you usually celebrate your birthday? • Did you celebrate birthdays differently when you were a child? • Do you think birthdays are more important for children or adults? • Do you like receiving birthday messages? Topic: Maps • Do you prefer paper maps or maps on a screen? • Have you ever drawn a map for someone? • Were maps used in your lessons at school? • Are you good at reading maps? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a time when you got lost. You should say: • where you were • how you got lost • what you did to find your way • and explain how you felt about the experience. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Would you say you have a good memory for routes? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Finding the way • What makes some people better than others at finding their way around? • Is it a good idea to ask strangers for directions? • How could towns be made easier for visitors to find their way around? Exploring new places • What is the appeal of exploring a city without a plan? • Are young people more adventurous travellers than older people, in your view? • What can people learn from visiting unfamiliar places? END OF TEST

Tidiness: An Overrated Virtue? In recent years, tidiness has acquired an almost moral significance. Bestselling books promise that clearing out our cupboards will transform our lives; television programmes show families weeping with relief as their possessions are carried away; and social media is full of photographs of spotless kitchens and perfectly organised drawers. The message is clear: a cluttered home reflects a cluttered mind, and order is the route to happiness. Entire businesses now exist to help people sort, store and discard their belongings. I want to suggest that this message, while not entirely wrong, is considerably exaggerated, and that a little mess deserves a better reputation. Let me begin with what the research does show. In one widely reported study, people were asked to describe their homes, and those who used words such as 'cluttered' and 'unfinished' were found to have higher levels of a stress hormone over the course of the day, and their mood tended to worsen as the evening went on. It would be foolish to dismiss such findings. For some people, a home overflowing with unused objects is a genuine source of anxiety, and for a small number, the inability to throw anything away is a serious psychological condition that requires professional help. But it is a large step from these findings to the claim that everyone should aim for minimalism. The study I have just described was relatively small, and it measured how people felt about their homes rather than how untidy the homes actually were. It is quite possible that people who are already stressed are more likely to notice, and to resent, the mess around them. Untidiness may be a symptom of a busy life rather than its cause. There is also evidence that disorder can have benefits. In a series of experiments at an American university, participants were placed either in a neat office or in one with papers and books scattered about. Those in the tidy room were more likely to choose a healthy snack and to make a donation to charity, which suggests that order encourages conventional, well-behaved choices. However, when asked to think of new uses for an everyday object, the participants in the messy room produced ideas that independent judges rated as more creative. Disorder, the researchers suggested, may encourage people to break away from convention. The researchers were careful to point out that neither kind of room was better overall; each simply encouraged a different way of thinking. Anyone who has worked in an office will also recognise that the person with the untidiest desk is not necessarily the least organised. Researchers who study how people manage information distinguish between 'filers', who put documents away in a system of folders, and 'pilers', who leave them in heaps on their desks. Pilers are often criticised, yet their piles are frequently arranged by an informal logic: the documents they are working on are near the top, and those that are no longer needed gradually sink to the bottom. Filers, by contrast, sometimes store documents so carefully that they forget they have them. Indeed, some pilers argue that putting a document out of sight is the surest way to forget about it. Finally, there is the question of time. Keeping a home or an office in perfect order requires constant effort, and the hours spent tidying, sorting and labelling are hours not spent with friends, on hobbies or simply resting. It is worth asking how many of those hours are really necessary, and whose standards they are meant to satisfy. For many families with young children, a perfectly tidy house is an unrealistic goal, and the pressure to achieve it can itself become a source of guilt and conflict. None of this is an argument for squalor. Dirty dishes, lost bills and floors that cannot be crossed without danger are nobody's idea of a good life. But between the show home and the rubbish tip there is a wide range of acceptable conditions, and where each person feels comfortable within that range is largely a matter of temperament. Instead of treating tidiness as a virtue and mess as a failing, we might simply accept that people differ, and that a desk covered in papers may belong to someone who knows exactly where everything is. Those in the tidy room were more likely to choose a healthy snack and to make a donation to charity, which suggests that order encourages conventional, well-behaved choices. However, when asked to think of new uses for an everyday object, the participants in the messy room produced ideas that independent judges rated as more creative. Disorder, the researchers suggested, may encourage people to break away from convention. The researchers were careful to point out that neither kind of room was better overall; each simply encouraged a different way of thinking. Anyone who has worked in an office will also recognise that the person with the untidiest desk is not necessarily the least organised. Researchers who study how people manage information distinguish between 'filers', who put documents away in a system of folders, and 'pilers', who leave them in heaps on their desks. Pilers are often criticised, yet their piles are frequently arranged by an informal logic: the documents they are working on are near the top, and those that are no longer needed gradually sink to the bottom. Filers, by contrast, sometimes store documents so carefully that they forget they have them. Indeed, some pilers argue that putting a document out of sight is the surest way to forget about it. Finally, there is the question of time. Keeping a home or an office in perfect order requires constant effort, and the hours spent tidying, sorting and labelling are hours not spent with friends, on hobbies or simply resting. It is worth asking how many of those hours are really necessary, and whose standards they are meant to satisfy. For many families with young children, a perfectly tidy house is an unrealistic goal, and the pressure to achieve it can itself become a source of guilt and conflict. None of this is an argument for squalor. Dirty dishes, lost bills and floors that cannot be crossed without danger are nobody's idea of a good life. But between the show home and the rubbish tip there is a wide range of acceptable conditions, and where each person feels comfortable within that range is largely a matter of temperament. Instead of treating tidiness as a virtue and mess as a failing, we might simply accept that people differ, and that a desk covered in papers may belong to someone who knows exactly where everything is. In recent years, sourdough has returned to fashion, and during periods when people were confined to their homes, internet searches for sourdough recipes rose dramatically around the world. When flour and water are mixed and left at room temperature, microorganisms already present in the flour, and on the baker's hands and in the surrounding air, begin to multiply. The yeasts produce the carbon dioxide gas that makes the dough rise, while the bacteria produce acids that give sourdough its characteristic sour taste and help to prevent the growth of mould. Bakers 'feed' their starters regularly with fresh flour and water, discarding part of the mixture each time, which keeps the microbes active and the community in balance. options.en: It is removed from the collection. READING PASSAGE 3 (Questions 27-40) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below. Small Talk, Big Rewards Few social activities have a worse reputation than small talk. Conversations about the weather, the traffic or the weekend are widely regarded as a tedious ritual, something to be endured at parties and in lifts until a more meaningful topic can be found. Many people say that they dislike it, and some popular writers on personality have argued that it is particularly exhausting for introverts. I want to argue that small talk is more valuable than its reputation suggests, and that we would all benefit from doing a little more of it. Consider first the evidence from research on everyday encounters. In one well-known series of experiments, commuters on trains and buses in an American city were asked either to start a conversation with a stranger, to sit in silence, or to behave as they normally would. Before the journey, most participants predicted that talking to a stranger would be the least pleasant option. In fact, those who talked reported the most enjoyable journeys, and none of them reported being rejected. Even participants who described themselves as shy enjoyed the conversations more than they had expected. The researchers concluded that people systematically underestimate how much others will want to talk to them, and how much they themselves will enjoy it. Other studies point in the same direction. Customers who exchanged a few friendly words with a barista when buying coffee reported a greater sense of belonging than those who kept the transaction as brief as possible. People who interact with a wider range of acquaintances during the day, from neighbours to shop assistants, tend to report better moods on those days, even when the interactions are very short. These relationships, which sociologists sometimes call 'weak ties', appear to contribute more to our wellbeing than we tend to assume. In another experiment, passers-by who were ignored by a stranger felt less connected to others than those who received a brief smile. Admittedly, one widely reported study seemed to suggest the opposite. Researchers who recorded fragments of participants' daily conversations found that the happiest people spent less time in small talk and more time in deeper, more substantive conversations. This finding is often quoted as evidence that small talk is worthless. But later attempts to repeat the study with larger groups found that the link between small talk and unhappiness largely disappeared. Substantive conversation does seem to be good for us, but that does not mean small talk is bad. Indeed, small talk is often the route by which deeper conversations begin. Very few friendships start with a discussion of the meaning of life; they start with a remark about the weather or a question about where someone bought their coat. Small talk allows people to signal goodwill, to judge whether the other person is interested in talking, and to discover shared interests at little risk. Small talk also follows predictable patterns, which is precisely why it feels safe: both people know roughly what is expected of them. Without it, the step to more meaningful conversation would be far more difficult. There are practical benefits too. In the workplace, brief informal conversations help colleagues to build trust, and people who know a little about each other's lives are more likely to cooperate and to ask for help when they need it. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Stationery • Do you prefer writing with a pen or a pencil? • Do you buy stationery often? • Did you collect any stationery when you were a child? • Which piece of stationery could you not do without? Topic: Napping • Do you ever take a nap during the day? • Is napping common in your country? • After a short nap, do you feel better or worse? • Should workplaces allow employees to nap? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a time when you helped a stranger. You should say: • who the person was • where you met them • what help you gave • and explain how you felt afterwards. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Do people in your town often help strangers? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Kindness • Is it more important to be kind to family or to strangers? • Are people less kind in big cities than in villages, in your opinion? • How can parents teach children to be kind? Helping in the community • What kinds of help do older people in your community need? • Should schools reward pupils for helping others? • Has technology made it easier or harder for people to help each other? Insurance in the Freezer: The World's Seed Banks A In the 1840s, a disease destroyed the potato crop in Ireland year after year, and around a million people died. One reason for the scale of the disaster was that most Irish farmers grew a single variety, the Lumper, which had no resistance to the disease. Modern agriculture has, in some respects, repeated the same mistake on a global scale. As farmers have switched to a small number of high-yielding varieties, thousands of traditional ones have disappeared from fields. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization has estimated that about three-quarters of the genetic diversity of crops was lost during the twentieth century. Yet this diversity is exactly what plant breeders need when they search for genes that can protect crops against new diseases, pests or a changing climate. B The idea of collecting seeds systematically owes much to the Russian botanist Nikolai Vavilov, who in the 1920s and 1930s led expeditions across five continents and assembled one of the largest seed collections in the world at his institute in Leningrad. During the German siege of the city in the Second World War, members of his staff guarded the collection through a winter of terrible famine. Several of them died of starvation at their desks rather than eat the seeds and grain in their care. Vavilov himself did not live to see the end of the war: he had fallen out of favour with the Soviet authorities and died in prison in 1943. C Today there are more than a thousand seed banks around the world, and most follow broadly similar procedures. Seeds are cleaned, dried until they contain very little moisture, and sealed in airtight foil packets before being stored at around minus 18 degrees Celsius. Under these conditions, the seeds of many crops can remain alive for decades, and some for centuries. Because even frozen seeds slowly lose their ability to germinate, samples are tested at intervals, and when their viability falls, a few are planted to produce fresh seed. Not every plant can be stored this way, however. The seeds of some species, including avocado and cocoa, are killed by drying, and they must be kept as living plants or preserved by other, more costly methods. D The best known of all these facilities is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, which opened in 2008 on a remo

options.en: They store seeds at very low temperatures. READING PASSAGE 3 (Questions 27-40) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below. The Myth of Doing Two Things at Once Ask people whether they are good at multitasking and many will say that they are. Job advertisements still list it as a desirable skill, and a typical office worker may answer emails during meetings, keep a messaging app open while writing reports and glance at a phone while talking to colleagues. The assumption behind all this is that dividing attention lets us get more done. I believe that, for most of the tasks that matter, this assumption is mistaken, and that the habit of constant switching makes us slower, less accurate and, in the long run, less able to concentrate. The first point to make is that what we call multitasking is rarely doing two things at once. When both tasks require conscious thought, such as reading a document and following a conversation, the brain does not process them in parallel. Instead, it switches rapidly between them. Each switch carries a cost. Laboratory studies in which participants alternate between simple tasks, such as classifying numbers and classifying letters, consistently find that people respond more slowly and make more errors immediately after a switch than when they repeat the same task. The cost of a single switch may be only a fraction of a second, but in a working day filled with interruptions these fractions add up, and on complex tasks the delay is greater, because it takes time to rebuild a mental picture of where one was. What makes this especially troubling is that people seem to be poor judges of their own performance. In a widely cited study conducted at Stanford University, students who reported that they frequently used several forms of media at the same time were compared with those who rarely did so. Surprisingly, the heavy multitaskers performed worse on tests that required them to ignore irrelevant information, and they were slower at switching between tasks, the very skill they might be expected to have practised. The study could not show whether multitasking caused these weaknesses or whether people who are easily distracted are simply drawn to it, but either way, the confidence of the heavy multitaskers was not justified by their results. A small number of people do appear to be genuine exceptions. Researchers in Utah who tested participants on a driving simulator while they performed demanding memory tasks found that a tiny minority, about two and a half per cent of the sample, showed no decline at all. These so-called supertaskers are interesting to scientists precisely because they are so rare. The odds that any particular person belongs to this group are very low, and the many drivers who believe that they can safely use a phone at the wheel are, in all probability, wrong. It would be an exaggeration, however, to claim that we can never combine activities. When one of the activities is automatic, there is little or no cost. Most people can walk and hold a conversation, or fold laundry while listening to the radio, without any difficulty, because walking and folding make few demands on conscious attention. Some people even find that background music helps them to persist with dull, repetitive work. The problems arise when two activities compete for the same limited resource, as when we try to compose a message while listening to a lecture. If the evidence is so clear, why does multitasking feel productive? Part of the answer is that switching provides a constant supply of small rewards: each new message or notification offers something novel, and answering it gives a sense of progress, even if the important task is left unfinished. Another reason is that much of the cost is invisible. We notice the five messages we answered, not the hour of focused work that never happened. The practical conclusions are straightforward, if not always easy to follow. Rather than responding to messages as they arrive, it is more efficient to deal with them in batches at set times. Notifications can be switched off during periods of concentrated work, and meetings can be held without laptops. Organisations, too, have a role to play: a workplace that expects instant replies effectively requires its staff to multitask. None of this means returning to some imagined golden age of uninterrupted thought. It simply means recognising that attention is a limited resource and spending it with more care. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Gifts • Do you enjoy choosing gifts for other people? • Can you remember a gift you received recently? • Do people in your country give gifts on special occasions? • Is it better to give money or an object as a gift? Topic: Trees • Are there many trees where you live? • Did you ever climb trees in your early years? • Which tree do you remember best from where you grew up? • Should cities plant more trees? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a public event that you attended and enjoyed. You should say: • what the event was • where and when it took place • who you went with • and explain why you enjoyed it. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Do you think you will attend that event again in future? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Public events • Why do towns and cities organise free public events? • Are large events always good for the local area? • Should local residents have a say in which events are held? Celebrations and tradition • How have public celebrations changed since your grandparents were young? • Why do some traditional festivals become less popular over time? • Will people still attend events in person in the future, or will they watch them online? END OF TEST

options.en: They had little effect on regeneration. READING PASSAGE 3 (Questions 27-40) You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below. Should We Trust Our First Impressions? Within moments of meeting someone, we have already formed a view of them. We decide whether they seem friendly or cold, competent or careless, trustworthy or not, often before they have said anything of substance. Popular books have celebrated this ability, suggesting that our snap judgements are a kind of hidden wisdom which we ignore at our peril. My own view is more cautious. First impressions are certainly fast, and sometimes surprisingly accurate, but they are far less reliable than we like to believe, and treating them as wisdom can lead us badly astray. There is no doubt about the speed. In experiments in which people are shown photographs of unfamiliar faces for as little as a tenth of a second, their ratings of qualities such as trustworthiness are very similar to the ratings given by people who were allowed to look for as long as they liked. Giving people more time, it seems, makes them more confident in their judgements, but hardly changes the judgements themselves. The mind, in other words, reaches its conclusion almost at once and then stops reconsidering it. Nor is there any doubt that these quick judgements sometimes contain real information. In a well-known study from the 1990s, students watched short silent video clips of university teachers they had never met, and rated them on qualities such as enthusiasm and warmth. Their ratings, based on a few seconds of footage, were remarkably similar to the end-of-course evaluations given by students who had been taught by those teachers for a whole term. Body language and facial expression evidently convey a good deal about how a person is likely to behave in a familiar setting such as a classroom. Similar results have since been reported for brief recordings of doctors talking to patients and of salespeople talking to customers. The difficulty is that our snap judgements are much better at some things than others. They are reasonably good at detecting how outgoing a person is, a quality that shows itself readily in behaviour. They are much worse at detecting honesty, intelligence or reliability, which are precisely the qualities we most need to know about when we choose a business partner, an employee or a friend. Part of the problem is that we rely on crude rules of thumb: faces with rounded features and large eyes, for example, tend to be judged as innocent and warm, whatever the character of their owners. When researchers compare first impressions of trustworthiness with measures of how people actually behave, the connection is generally weak. People whose faces are judged to look trustworthy are not, on the whole, more honest than anyone else. Worse, these judgements can have real consequences. Studies of elections have found that photographs of candidates which strangers judged to look more competent belonged, more often than chance would predict, to the candidates who went on to win. Since a face is no guide to how well someone would perform in office, this is a troubling finding. Similar effects have been reported in decisions about hiring, and even in the severity of sentences in criminal courts. A further problem is that first impressions are remarkably persistent. Once we have formed a view, we tend to notice information that confirms it and to explain away information that does not. A candidate who makes a poor start in an interview may struggle to recover, because the interviewer unconsciously interprets every later answer in the light of that first moment. A nervous pause that would be forgiven in a candidate who started well becomes, in one who started badly, further evidence of unsuitability. This is one reason why many organisations now use structured interviews, in which every candidate is asked the same questions and the answers are scored against agreed criteria. Such interviews have consistently been found to predict job performance better than informal conversations. None of this means that we should, or could, stop forming first impressions. They are an automatic part of how we perceive other people. What we can do is treat them as hypotheses rather than conclusions: provisional ideas to be tested against further evidence. A first impression that survives a second and third meeting may well be correct. One that is never questioned is simply a prejudice that happened to arrive early.
