prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Shoes • Do you prefer comfortable shoes or fashionable ones? • How often do you buy new shoes? • Have you ever bought shoes online? • Is it normal to take your shoes off indoors where you come from? Topic: Being on time • Are you usually on time? • Does it annoy you if friends keep you waiting? • Is being on time important in your culture? • If you realise you'll be late, how do you let people know? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a building in your town or city that you find interesting. You should say: • where the building is • what it looks like • what it is used for • and explain why you find it interesting. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Do many tourists visit this building? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Architecture • Why do some people dislike modern buildings? • Should governments protect old buildings, even when they are expensive to maintain? • How can architects make cities more pleasant to live in? Housing and the future • Is living in a flat better than living in a house? • Why are homes in big cities so expensive? • How might the homes people live in change in the next half-century? END OF TEST

prompt.en: For decades, timekeepers were too __________ for most ships READING PASSAGE 2 You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below. Holding Back the Sea: Venice and its Flood Barrier A Venice has always lived with water. Built on more than a hundred small islands in a shallow lagoon at the northern end of the Adriatic Sea, the city has for centuries experienced what Venetians call acqua alta, or high water: unusually high tides that spill over the edges of canals and flood the streets and squares. Such floods occur when strong tides combine with low atmospheric pressure and winds blowing up the Adriatic from the south-east, which push water towards the lagoon. Salt water is particularly damaging, because it gradually eats into the brick and stone of the lower walls of buildings, many of which rest on wooden piles driven deep into the mud. Residents have traditionally coped by raising their furniture, installing barriers across doorways and walking on temporary wooden platforms laid out along the main routes. B The problem has, however, become more serious over time. During the twentieth century the city sank, partly because large quantities of groundwater were pumped from beneath the lagoon for industry. That pumping was stopped in the 1970s, and the sinking has slowed considerably, but by then the damage had been done. At the same time, the sea itself has been rising. The result is that floods which were once rare are now frequent, and many ground floors that were once used as shops or homes have been abandoned because they are flooded so often. In November 1966, a flood reached nearly two metres above normal sea level and caused enormous damage; in November 2019 a tide of 187 centimetres, the second highest ever recorded, flooded more than 80 per cent of the city. C The 1966 disaster prompted calls for a permanent solution, but decades of debate followed before construction began in 2003. The system eventually built is known as MOSE. Slow Travel and Its Rewards For most of the history of travel, the journey was the main event. A trip from one European capital to another took days, and travellers wrote at length about the landscapes they crossed, the people they met on the way and the inns where they stayed. Today, for many of us, the journey has shrunk to an inconvenience to be endured: a few hours in an airport and an aircraft cabin, followed by the sudden arrival in a place that may be thousands of kilometres from home. I want to suggest that, where we have the choice, we would often do better to travel more slowly. The most obvious argument is environmental. Aviation currently accounts for only a few per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, but for an individual traveller a single long-haul return flight can produce more emissions than many people in poorer countries generate in a whole year. Over shorter distances, a train journey typically produces a small fraction of the emissions of the equivalent flight, especially where railways run on electricity from low-carbon sources. I do not believe that people should never fly; for intercontinental journeys there is often no practical alternative. But many flights within a continent could be replaced without great hardship, particularly now that night trains, which allow passengers to cover long distances while they sleep, have returned to a number of European routes. The objection, of course, is time. A journey that takes two hours by air may take eight or ten by rail. But the comparison is less straightforward than it appears. Flight times rarely include the journey to an airport on the edge of a city, the security checks and the waiting at the gate, whereas many trains run from the centre of one city to the centre of another. More importantly, time on a train is not necessarily wasted. One can read, work, talk to fellow passengers or simply watch the countryside change, activities that are difficult in the cramped and noisy conditions of an aircraft. There is also a psychological argument, which I find the most persuasive. When we arrive somewhere by air, we often feel disoriented, as if we had been transported rather than had travelled. Moving gradually through changing landscapes, seeing the architecture, the vegetation and even the language on signs alter along the way, gives us a sense of where a place is in relation to others. The destination becomes part of a continuous geography rather than an isolated point. Several travel writers have described this as arriving in a place properly, and I think they are right. Even the gradual change in temperature and light over a long journey helps the body and mind to adjust. Slow travel also tends to change what we do when we arrive. Travellers who have invested a day or two in reaching a place are more likely to stay longer, and less likely to rush from one famous sight to another. Longer stays in fewer places spread the economic benefits of tourism more widely, to small towns along the route as well as to the destination, where a traveller who stops for a night may discover somewhere they would never have thought of visiting, and reduce the pressure on the handful of famous cities that are currently overwhelmed by short-stay visitors. I accept that slow travel is not available to everyone. Many people have only a few days of holiday a year, and for them a long overland journey may simply be impossible. Families with young children, too, may reasonably feel that a day spent in transit is more than they can manage. Rail fares, moreover, are often higher than budget airline tickets, a situation that reflects, in part, the fact that aviation fuel is untaxed in many countries. Until these imbalances are addressed, it would be unfair to criticise people who choose the cheapest and quickest option. Nevertheless, for those who do have the time and the means, I would argue that the slow journey deserves reconsideration, not as a sacrifice made for the sake of the planet, but as a better way of travelling in its own right. The question to ask is not only how quickly we can get somewhere, but what we want the experience of getting there to be. Questions 27-30: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Flowers • Do you like having flowers at home? • Are flowers given as gifts in your country? • Is there a flower that is special to you? • Have you ever grown flowers yourself? Topic: Getting around • How do you usually travel around your town? • Is public transport in your area reliable? • Did you use buses or trains much as a child? • What would make you use public transport more often? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a time when you were very busy. You should say: • when it was • why you were so busy • how you managed your time • and explain how you felt during this time. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Do you enjoy being busy? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Work and free time • Why do many people feel that they have too little free time? • Should employers limit the hours their staff work? • Is it possible to have a good balance between work and the rest of life? Planning and time • Do you think people plan their time better now than in the past? • Can planning every hour of the day cause problems? • How can schools teach young people to manage their time? END OF TEST

Counting Steps in the Desert: How Ants Find Their Way Home A In the salt flats of North Africa, the ground temperature at midday can exceed 60 degrees Celsius, a heat that would kill most insects within minutes. Yet this is precisely the time when one remarkable group of insects, the desert ants of the genus Cataglyphis, leave their nests to search for food. They are scavengers, feeding mainly on the bodies of other insects that have died of heat exhaustion, and by foraging in the hottest part of the day they avoid the lizards that would otherwise prey on them. Their long legs keep their bodies a few millimetres above the scorching surface, where the air is slightly cooler, and they run remarkably fast, covering many times their own body length every second. Even so, an ant that stays out too long will die, so it cannot afford to waste time. B The difficulty these ants face is that their environment offers few landmarks, and their nests are mere holes in the ground. Moreover, they forage alone and do not lay scent trails, as many other ants do, because the heat would cause the scent to evaporate quickly. A foraging ant may wander for more than a hundred metres, following a winding, apparently random path. But as soon as it finds food, it turns and runs almost directly back to its nest. For a creature only about a centimetre long, this is an extraordinary feat of navigation, comparable to a person walking several kilometres across a featureless plain and then heading straight home without a map. C The secret is a technique that sailors call dead reckoning, and biologists call path integration. Throughout its outward journey, the ant continuously keeps track of the direction and distance it has travelled, and from these it calculates a 'home vector', the direction and distance that will take it straight back to the nest. The importance of this vector was demonstrated by simple experiments. When an ant that had just found food was picked up and moved a few metres to one side, it ran in the direction and for the distance that would have taken it home from its original position. Arriving at an empty spot, it began a systematic search, running in loops of increasing size until it found the nest. D The ants obtain their sense of direction from the sky. Paying Children for Chores: A Good Idea? Few questions divide parents as reliably as whether children should be paid for doing household chores. In some families, pocket money is earned task by task: so much for washing the car, so much for emptying the dishwasher. In others, children receive a fixed weekly allowance regardless of what they do, and are simply expected to help around the house. Both camps can claim good intentions. Those who pay for chores say they are teaching children that money must be earned; those who do not say they are teaching children that a family is not a business. I want to argue that the second group has the better case, though with some important qualifications. The case for paying is easy to understand. Adults are paid for their work, and children who learn to link effort with reward may be better prepared for adult life. Payment also gives parents a simple way of encouraging behaviour they want, without arguments. And children who earn their money, it is sometimes said, value it more and spend it more carefully. These are reasonable arguments, and I do not dismiss them; my disagreement lies in what is being paid for. My first objection is that paying for basic chores changes the meaning of the task. Clearing the table after a meal or keeping one's room tidy are things that every member of a household does because they share the space, not because they are employed. Once a price is attached, a child may reasonably conclude that such tasks are optional: if he does not need the money this week, why should he do them? Parents who have tried payment schemes often report exactly this. The child who has saved enough for a new game simply announces that he will not be doing the dishes, and the parent has no answer except to raise the price. A system intended to encourage cooperation ends up encouraging bargaining instead. There is also some evidence that rewards can reduce children's interest in activities that they would otherwise have done willingly. In a well-known experiment from the 1970s, nursery-school children who enjoyed drawing were divided into groups. Those who were promised a reward for drawing later spent less of their free time drawing than children who had received no reward or an unexpected one. The researchers suggested that the promised reward had turned an enjoyable activity into a form of work. The experiment did not, of course, involve household chores, and we should be careful about drawing firm conclusions from it. But it does suggest that payment may undermine, rather than build, a sense of responsibility. None of this means that children should receive no money at all. On the contrary, I believe that a regular allowance, not linked to chores, is one of the best ways of teaching children to manage money. A child who receives a fixed sum each week has to make decisions: whether to spend it at once or save for something larger, and what to do when it has run out. Mistakes made with small sums at the age of eight are far less costly than mistakes made with a first salary at twenty. The value of an allowance lies in these decisions, not in how the money was obtained. Where, then, does paid work fit in? I see no harm in paying children for jobs that go beyond the ordinary contribution expected of every household member, such as washing the family car or helping to paint a fence. Such arrangements resemble real employment, with an agreed task and an agreed price, and they can teach children something about negotiation and reliability. The essential point is to keep the two categories separate, so that a child never comes to believe that ordinary help around the house is a service to be bought and sold. In the end, families must decide for themselves, and children brought up under either system can turn out to be responsible and generous adults. But if the goal is to raise children who help because they understand that they belong to a household, and who also know how to handle money, it makes sense to teach these two lessons separately rather than combining them in a single weekly payment. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: Handwriting • Do you write by hand very often? • Is your handwriting easy to read? • Were you taught joined-up writing as a pupil? • Do you think children still need to learn to write by hand? Topic: Photographs • Do you like taking photographs? • What do you usually do with the photos you take? • Would you rather be in photos or take them? • Are there any old family photographs that are important to you? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a website or app that you use often. You should say: • what it is • how you found out about it • what you use it for • and explain why you find it useful. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Would you recommend this to older relatives? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) The internet and information • How do most people in your country find news today? • Is it a problem that so much information online is free? • How can people tell whether information on the internet is reliable? Technology and young people • Should there be limits on how long children spend using apps? • What skills do young people learn from using technology? • Will apps take over some kinds of work one day? END OF TEST

The Vanishing Dark A For almost all of history, night meant darkness. Today, for most people in industrialised countries, it does not. Street lights, illuminated buildings, car headlights and advertising screens produce a glow that spreads far beyond the places where it is needed, and on cloudy nights it is reflected back to the ground. A widely cited study published in 2016 estimated that more than 80 per cent of the world's population lives under skies affected by artificial light, and that the Milky Way can no longer be seen by more than a third of humanity. Satellite measurements show that the area of the Earth's surface that is artificially lit at night has continued to grow, by around two per cent a year in the period studied. B For astronomers, the consequences have long been obvious; many observatories built near cities in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries have had to give up serious research. But in recent decades, biologists have become increasingly concerned about the effects of artificial light on other living things. Life on Earth evolved with a reliable cycle of day and night, and a great many species use light levels to regulate their behaviour, from the timing of feeding and breeding to the direction in which they travel. Many animals are active only at night precisely because darkness protects them from predators, so even a modest increase in light can expose them to danger or keep them hidden in their shelters for longer, reducing the time available for feeding. The Uses of Failure in the Classroom It has become fashionable to say that failure is good for learners. Motivational posters in school corridors declare that mistakes are proof that you are trying, and books for teachers urge them to 'celebrate failure'. I have some sympathy with the message, but I am also uneasy about it, because it is often stated so vaguely that it is impossible to disagree with and difficult to act on. Not every failure is useful, and some are simply discouraging. The real question is what kinds of failure help students to learn, and under what conditions. Fortunately, there is now a reasonable body of research that allows us to begin answering it. One of the most interesting answers comes from research on what has been called productive failure. In a typical study, one group of students is taught a new mathematical method directly and then practises it. Another group is first given a challenging problem that requires the method, before they have been taught it, and asked to try to solve it on their own or in small groups. Unsurprisingly, most of the second group fail to find the correct solution. They are then taught the method in the usual way. Repeated studies, beginning with work in Singapore schools, have found that students in the second group often perform better on later tests that require them to understand the method and apply it to unfamiliar problems, although not necessarily on tests of routine calculation. Why should struggling with a problem one cannot yet solve be helpful? One explanation is that the attempt makes students aware of what they do not know. Having tried several approaches and discovered their limitations, they are better prepared to recognise why the correct method works when it is finally explained. Their failed attempts, in other words, prepare the ground for later learning. Students who are simply shown the method, by contrast, may learn to follow its steps without ever asking why those steps are necessary. This fits a wider body of research on what psychologists call 'desirable difficulties': conditions that make learning feel slower and harder at the time but lead to better long-term retention. It is important, however, to notice the conditions that make such failure productive. The problems in these studies are carefully designed: hard enough that students are unlikely to solve them, but not so hard that they cannot make a meaningful attempt. The struggle lasts for a limited time, usually a single lesson, and it is always followed by clear teaching. Students are not left to fail indefinitely, nor are they told that their failure is a sign of weakness. Remove these conditions, and the benefits are likely to disappear. This is where I part company with some of the more enthusiastic promoters of failure. Repeated failure without support is not productive; it is demoralising. A student who struggles with reading year after year, and who is told that this struggle is building character, is unlikely to be grateful. Nor is it clear that praising failure in general terms changes students' attitudes. Several large studies of programmes designed to teach students that ability can grow with effort have found effects that are real but considerably smaller than early, enthusiastic reports suggested. What, then, should teachers do? First, they should distinguish between failure that is designed and failure that is merely tolerated. Setting a challenging problem before teaching a new topic is a deliberate strategy; allowing students to fall behind without help is not. Second, they should make the purpose of the struggle clear, so that students understand that they are not expected to succeed at the first attempt. Third, and most importantly, they should ensure that every period of struggle is followed by feedback and explanation. Students who are allowed to struggle but never shown where they went wrong are likely to remember their errors rather than the correct method, which is the opposite of what the teacher intended. Failure, in short, is neither good nor bad in itself. It is a tool, and like any tool it can be used skilfully or clumsily. The slogans on the corridor walls are not wrong, exactly, but they are incomplete. A mistake becomes valuable only when someone helps the learner to understand it. prompt.en: 11-14 minutes · 3 parts Speaking test The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner and is recorded. It lasts 11-14 minutes. A recording of the examiner's prompts with timed pauses is provided in audio/speaking_examiner_prompts.mp3 for self-practice; record yourself answering. Part 1: Introduction and interview (4-5 minutes) The examiner asks about familiar topics. Topic: The night sky • Can you see many stars from where you live? • At school, were you taught about the stars and planets? • Is space travel something you'd like to try? • Do you prefer the night or the day? Topic: Puzzles • Do you enjoy doing puzzles? • What kinds of puzzles did you do as a child? • Do you prefer doing puzzles alone or with others? • Do you think puzzles are good for the brain? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a book that you found useful. You should say: • what the book was • when you read it • why you read it • and explain why it was so helpful. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Do you often recommend books to friends? Part 3: Two-way discussion (4-5 minutes) Reading habits • Do people in your country read less than they used to? • Why do some people prefer non-fiction to novels? • Should parents read to their children every day? Books and technology • Why do some people prefer reading on a screen? • Will printed books disappear in the future? • Are libraries in your city used differently now? END OF TEST

Why Do Zebras Have Stripes? A Few animals are as instantly recognisable as the zebra, yet the purpose of its black-and-white coat has puzzled biologists for more than 150 years. In the nineteenth century, Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, the two founders of the theory of evolution by natural selection, disagreed about it. Darwin doubted that the stripes had any practical use and suggested that they might have evolved because zebras found them attractive in a mate. Wallace believed they must have a survival value, perhaps by making zebras harder to see in long grass or at dusk. Since then, at least a dozen explanations have been proposed, and the debate has only recently begun to move towards a conclusion. Much of the progress has come not from simply observing zebras but from carefully designed field experiments. B The most popular traditional explanation was camouflage. Stripes, it was argued, might break up the outline of the animal, or might confuse a lion or hyena watching a running herd, making it hard to pick out a single target. However, research on the eyesight of predators has weakened this idea. A study published in 2016 calculated how zebras would appear to lions and hyenas, whose vision is less sharp than ours. It found that beyond about 50 metres in daylight, and at even shorter distances at dusk, the stripes would blur into a uniform grey, and that at such distances a predator would usually be able to hear or smell a zebra anyway. Moreover, lions appear to kill zebras at least as often as other prey of similar size. C A second idea is that stripes help to keep zebras cool. In theory, black stripes absorb more heat than white ones, and the difference in temperature could create small air currents over the skin. Some studies have found that zebras living in hotter regions tend to have bolder stripes. Yet experiments using barrels covered in striped and plain hides found no clear cooling effect, and many researchers now believe that, if stripes do affect body temperature, the effect is too small to explain their evolution. Measuring the temperature of a living zebra in the wild is also extremely difficult, which makes the question hard to settle. D A third suggestion is that stripes are a kind of identity badge. Each zebra's pattern is unique, like a human fin

Walking: An Undervalued Habit Walking is the most ordinary of human activities, and perhaps for that reason it is easy to underestimate. Most of us learn to do it before we can speak, and many of us then spend the rest of our lives trying to avoid it, driving short distances, taking lifts up a single floor and regarding a twenty-minute walk as an inconvenience. I want to argue that this attitude is a mistake, both for individuals and for the societies they live in, and that walking deserves to be taken far more seriously than it is. The health case is the easiest to make. Regular walking reduces the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and several kinds of cancer, and it appears to improve mood and sleep. Unlike many forms of exercise, it requires no equipment, no membership fee and no special skill. It is also, for most people, sustainable: someone who walks briskly for half an hour a day is far more likely to keep the habit for years than someone who joins a gym in January. Large studies that have followed thousands of people over many years have found that the more steps people take each day, the lower their risk of dying early, although the benefit appears to level off at a point that varies with age. It is worth pausing over the familiar target of 10,000 steps a day. This number did not come from medical research. It was popularised in Japan in the 1960s as part of the marketing of an early pedometer, whose name could be translated as 'ten thousand steps meter'. Recent research suggests that, for many older adults, the greatest benefits come at a lower figure, and that any increase in walking is valuable for people who are mostly inactive. I mention this not to dismiss step counting, which motivates many people, but to point out that an arbitrary target can discourage those who believe they will never reach it. The benefits of walking are not only physical. Many writers and thinkers, from philosophers in ancient Greece to modern novelists, have claimed that they think best on foot, and there is some experimental evidence that they are right. In one well-known study, people who were asked to suggest unusual uses for everyday objects produced considerably more ideas while walking, or shortly afterwards, than while sitting. Interestingly, walking on a treadmill facing a blank wall had much the same effect as walking outdoors, which suggests that the movement itself, not simply the change of scenery, is responsible. Walking may not help with every kind of thinking, but for generating new ideas it appears to be a remarkably effective tool. Why, then, do so many people walk so little? Laziness is the usual answer, but I believe that it is largely wrong. In many towns and cities, walking is not a practical choice. Housing estates are built far from shops and schools; pavements are narrow, broken or absent; busy roads can be crossed only by long detours. For decades, planners designed places for the convenience of drivers and then expressed surprise when residents chose to drive. People respond, quite reasonably, to the environment they find themselves in. Some readers will object that walking is not an option for everyone, and they are right. People with certain disabilities, or those who must travel long distances to work, cannot simply leave the car at home. Nothing I am proposing should make life harder for them. But a street that is safe and pleasant for a person walking is usually better for a wheelchair user too, and the more journeys that are made on foot, the less congested the roads become for those who genuinely need to drive. What would a society that took walking seriously look like? It would build homes within walking distance of everyday services. It would give pedestrians wide pavements, frequent crossings and shade from the sun. It would treat the ability of a child to walk safely to school as a basic measure of a well-designed neighbourhood. None of this requires new technology or vast public spending; much of it simply requires a change in priorities. Walking, after all, is the oldest form of transport we have. It may also turn out to be one of the most modern. Questions 27-30: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

Topic: Bags • What kind of bag do you usually carry? • What do you keep in your bag? • Can you remember losing a bag? • Do you think expensive bags are worth the money? Topic: Swimming • Can you swim? • Where do people usually swim in your area? • Did you have swimming lessons at school? • Would you rather swim in a pool or in the sea? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a place near water, such as a river, lake or the sea, that you enjoy visiting. You should say: • where it is • how often you go there • what you do there • and explain why you enjoy visiting it. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. The examiner may ask one brief follow-up question, e.g.: Do you usually go there on your own or in company? Grown-ups at Play Somewhere between childhood and adulthood, most of us stop playing. We may still play sport or games, but usually with a purpose: to keep fit, to win, to socialise or to fill an empty evening. The spontaneous, purposeless activity that fills so much of a child's day comes to seem faintly embarrassing in an adult, something to be indulged on holiday or hidden from colleagues. I want to suggest that this is a loss, and that we have much to gain from taking play more seriously. Defining play is notoriously difficult. In the 1930s, the Dutch historian Johan Huizinga described it as an activity that is freely chosen, separate from ordinary life, governed by its own rules and pursued for its own sake. Later researchers have offered many alternative definitions, but most agree on two features: play is voluntary, and it is done because it is enjoyable rather than to achieve some external goal. By that standard, a game of football played to impress a selector is not quite play, while doodling during a meeting might be. The definition matters, because it suggests that what counts as play depends less on the activity itself than on the attitude of the person doing it. Biologists have long been interested in why animals play, since play costs time and energy and can even be dangerous. Young animals that play fight, chase and wrestle may be practising skills they will need as adults, but this cannot be the whole explanation, because play is also common in adult animals of some species. One influential suggestion is that play trains animals to cope with the unexpected: by deliberately putting themselves in unpredictable situations, they learn to recover quickly from surprises. If that is right, play is not a luxury but a form of preparation for an uncertain world. It is worth noting that animals deprived of the chance to play when young often react poorly to new situations later in life, although the evidence for this comes largely from laboratory studies. There are reasons to think that the same may be true of humans. Many of the qualities that employers claim to value, such as creativity, flexibility and the ability to cooperate, are precisely those that play develops. Play also allows us to experiment without fear of failure, since its results do not matter in the way that the results of work do. It is no coincidence, I think, that so many scientific and artistic discoveries have emerged from people tinkering with ideas for their own amusement rather than following a plan. Yet adult life is organised in ways that squeeze play out. Long working hours leave little free time, and the time that remains is increasingly filled with activities that have a purpose attached: exercise that is tracked and measured, hobbies that are turned into side businesses, holidays that are planned to the last detail and shared online. Even children's play has become more structured, with organised clubs and classes replacing the unsupervised outdoor play that was common a generation ago. I do not wish to romanticise the past, which had dangers of its own, but something valuable has been lost, and it is adults, not children, who are responsible for that loss. Some companies have responded by introducing games and playful spaces into the workplace, with table tennis tables and brightly coloured meeting rooms. I am sceptical. Play that is required by an employer, or designed to increase productivity, is no longer freely chosen, and so it loses much of what makes it valuable. A worker who is told to have fun at a team-building event is not playing; he or she is performing a task. The playful office may look attractive in photographs, but it can easily become another way of extending the working day. What, then, can be done? Mostly, I think, adults need to give themselves permission. Play does not require expensive equipment or special skills. It can mean singing in the kitchen, building something pointless, joining in a children's game in the park, or simply wandering without a destination. The essential thing is that it is done for its own sake. In a culture that measures the value of every hour, there is something quietly radical about doing something simply because it is enjoyable. Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a game or sport that you enjoyed playing as a child. Lessons from the Termite Mound A Across the savannahs of southern and eastern Africa rise some of the most impressive structures built by any animal other than humans. The mounds of fungus-growing termites can reach several metres in height and may be occupied for decades, and some are so large that they are visible in satellite images. Yet the mound itself is not where the termites live. The colony, which may contain millions of insects, occupies an underground nest beneath it. The tall structure above ground appears to serve another purpose: controlling the air in the nest below. Inside, the mound is riddled with a network of tunnels, from a broad central passage to narrow channels just beneath the surface, and its shape and size vary considerably from one region to another. B These termites do not digest wood or grass directly. Instead, they carry plant material into the nest and use it to cultivate a fungus, which breaks the material down; the termites then feed on the fungus and its products. The fungus is sensitive to its environment and grows best in stable conditions. A large colony also consumes a great deal of oxygen and produces large amounts of carbon dioxide, which must somehow be removed. Without an effective exchange of gases between the nest and the outside air, the colony would suffocate. The termites also need to keep the nest humid, since both they and their fungus dry out easily, so the problem is not simply one of letting fresh air in. C For many years, scientists believed they understood how this exchange worked. According to an explanation proposed in the 1960s, warm air produced by the colony's activity rose through a large central chimney and escaped through the walls of the mound, while fresh air was drawn in near the base. The mound, in other words, was thought to work like a natural air-conditioning system, driven by the heat of the colony itself. The explanation was elegant and widely repeated in textbooks, although it was based on relatively few direct measurements of air movement inside real mounds. D Recent research suggests that the reality is more complicated. Studies in Namibia found that the mound's walls are porous, allowing gases to pass through them slowly, and that the wind blowing across the mound plays an important part in moving air within it. Star Ratings and Their Limits: The Problem with Online Reviews Before booking a hotel, choosing a restaurant or buying a kettle, most of us now consult the opinions of strangers. Online reviews have become one of the most influential sources of information in modern life, and for good reason: they offer the experience of hundreds or thousands of customers rather than the claims of a seller. Yet the more closely researchers examine these reviews, the clearer it becomes that the star ratings we rely on are a far less accurate guide than they appear. The first problem is who writes reviews in the first place. Most customers never review anything at all, however satisfied or disappointed they are. Those who do tend to be those with strong feelings, either delighted or furious, and so the distribution of ratings on many websites is strangely shaped. Instead of most ratings clustering around the middle, as one might expect if they reflected the full range of customer experience, there is usually a large peak at five stars, a smaller peak at one star, and relatively few ratings in between. The average of such a distribution can be misleading, because it combines two very different groups of people. A product with an average of three stars might be one that everyone finds acceptable, or one that half its buyers love and half hate, and the single number cannot tell us which. A second problem is that reviews influence one another. In a well-known experiment, researchers working with a news website randomly gave some newly posted comments a single positive vote. Those comments went on to receive significantly higher ratings than comments that had received no artificial vote, as later readers were swayed by what they believed others had thought. Similar effects have been observed for products: a few early positive reviews can make later reviewers more generous, and a few early negative ones can damage a product's reputation regardless of its quality. Third, there is the inflation of ratings over time. On many platforms, the average rating is now so high that anything below four and a half stars is treated with suspicion. This is partly because businesses actively encourage satisfied customers to leave reviews, and partly because some customers feel uncomfortable giving low marks to individuals, such as drivers or hosts, whose livelihoods may depend on them. On some platforms, a rating of three stars, which might once have meant 'satisfactory', is now interpreted by many users as a sign of serious problems. When almost everything is rated highly, ratings cease to distinguish between the excellent and the merely adequate. Finally, and most seriously, there are fake reviews. Some businesses pay for positive reviews of their own products or negative reviews of competitors' products, and an entire industry has grown up to supply them. Platforms remove large numbers of suspicious reviews every year, and several governments have introduced laws that make buying or selling fake reviews illegal. Detecting them, however, is difficult, and nobody knows precisely how many remain. Writers of fake reviews have learned to imitate the style of genuine customers, mentioning small faults to appear balanced, and the use of computer programs that generate fluent text has made the task of spotting them harder still. None of this means that reviews are worthless. I would argue, though, that we need to read them differently. The written comments are often more useful than the star rating, particularly the moderate reviews, which tend to describe both strengths and weaknesses. The number of reviews matters as much as the average: a rating of 4.8 based on five reviews tells us very little. And it is worth asking whether the problems that reviewers mention are ones that matter to us; a hotel criticised for being too quiet may be exactly what one traveller is looking for. Online reviews were supposed to give power to consumers, and to some extent they have. But they have also created a system that can be manipulated, and in which a small and unrepresentative group of people shapes the choices of everyone else. Treating reviews as one piece of evidence among many, rather than as a final verdict, is the best protection we have, alongside the advice of people we actually know and trust. Topic: Hats • Do you ever wear a hat? • Are hats in fashion in your country at the moment? • Did you wear a hat as part of a school uniform? • Why do people wear hats? Topic: Snacks • What snacks do you like? • Do you eat more snacks now than when you were younger? • Do you think snacks are bad for people's health? • Which snacks do people in your country like most? Part 2: Individual long turn (3-4 minutes, including 1 minute of preparation) Describe a purchase that you were very pleased with. You should say: • what it was • where you bought it • how you chose it • and explain why you were pleased with it. You will have 1 minute to prepare and may make notes. Then speak for 1-2 minutes. Time to Stop Changing the Clocks Twice a year, in much of Europe and North America, hundreds of millions of people move their clocks forward or back by an hour. Most of us grumble, adjust, and forget about it until the next time. For a few days our sleep is disturbed, we arrive early or late for appointments, and we search for the settings on the clocks in our cars and kitchens that we have not changed since the previous season. But the practice of daylight saving time, as it is called in some countries, is neither natural nor inevitable, and I believe the case for continuing it has become very weak. The idea is older than many people realise. In 1907 a British builder, William Willett, published a pamphlet complaining that people wasted the bright early hours of summer mornings asleep, and proposing that clocks be advanced in stages during the spring. He campaigned for the idea until his death in 1915 but did not see it adopted. It was Germany that first introduced summer time nationally, in 1916, during the First World War, in order to save coal; Britain and many other countries followed within weeks or months. After the war, several countries abandoned the practice, only to reintroduce it during later emergencies, and it was not until the energy crises of the 1970s that it became a permanent feature of life across most of Europe. Saving energy, then, was the original justification, and it is still the one most often heard. Yet modern evidence suggests that the savings are small at best. Lighting accounts for a much smaller share of energy use than it did a century ago, and in hot regions, lighter evenings may increase the use of air conditioning. One study, which took advantage of the fact that some counties in the American state of Indiana adopted daylight saving time later than others, found that the change actually increased household electricity consumption slightly. Against these modest benefits must be set some real costs. Changing the clocks disrupts the body's internal clock, and the spring change, which takes away an hour, is particularly hard. Several studies have reported a rise in heart attacks in the days immediately after it, and some have found an increase in road accidents. The effect on any single person is small, but when it is multiplied across a whole population it is not trivial. Many people also report feeling tired and irritable for days afterwards. Farmers, whose animals do not follow the clock, have long complained about the disruption, and parents of young children often find that it takes a week or more for their children's sleep to settle. Public opinion appears to agree. In 2018 the European Commission held a public consultation, and of the more than four million people who responded, a large majority wanted the clock changes to end. The following year, the European Parliament voted in favour of abolishing them. However, member states could not agree on how to proceed, and at the time of writing the clocks in Europe are still changing twice a year. Part of the difficulty is that ending the changes requires a choice: should the clocks stay permanently on summer time or permanently on standard time? Permanent summer time is popular because it gives lighter evenings all year round. But it would also mean very dark winter mornings, especially in northern and western regions, where in midwinter the sun might not rise until well after nine o'clock. Many sleep scientists therefore favour permanent standard time, which keeps clock time more closely aligned with the sun. They argue that morning light is particularly important for keeping the body's internal clock in step with the day. I share their view, though I recognise that it would be less popular. What matters most, however, is that the twice-yearly disruption should end. A system introduced to save coal in wartime has long outlived its purpose. It survives largely through habit and the difficulty of coordinating a change between neighbouring countries. These are poor reasons to keep imposing a small but real cost on hundreds of millions of people every year. It is time for governments to agree on a single time and to stick to it permanently. Farmers, whose animals do not follow the clock, have long complained about the disruption, and parents of young children often find that it takes a week or more for their children's sleep to settle. Public opinion appears to agree. In 2018 the European Commission held a public consultation, and of the more than four million people who responded, a large majority wanted the clock changes to end. The following year, the European Parliament voted in favour of abolishing them. However, member states could not agree on how to proceed, and at the time of writing the clocks in Europe are still changing twice a year. Part of the difficulty is that ending the changes requires a choice: should the clocks stay permanently on summer time or permanently on standard time? Permanent summer time is popular because it gives lighter evenings all year round. But it would also mean very dark winter mornings, especially in northern and western regions, where in midwinter the sun might not rise until well after nine o'clock. Many sleep scientists therefore favour permanent standard time, which keeps clock time more closely aligned with the sun. They argue that morning light is particularly important for keeping the body's internal clock in step with the day. I share their view, though I recognise that it would be less popular. What matters most, however, is that the twice-yearly disruption should end. A system introduced to save coal in wartime has long outlived its purpose. It survives largely through habit and the difficulty of coordinating a change between neighbouring countries. These are poor reasons to keep imposing a small but real cost on hundreds of millions of people every year. It is time for governments to agree on a single time and to stick to it permanently. The Axolotl: A Laboratory Star in Danger A The axolotl is a salamander, an amphibian related to frogs and newts, but it differs from most of its relatives in one striking way. Most amphibians undergo a dramatic change as they mature, losing the gills they used to breathe underwater as larvae and developing lungs so that they can live on land. The axolotl usually does not. It reaches adulthood and breeds while keeping many of its juvenile features, including the feathery external gills that sprout from the sides of its head. This ability to remain in a larval form for life is known as neoteny. Adult axolotls usually grow to between fifteen and thirty centimetres in length, and in the wild they are generally dark brown or grey, with small gold flecks; the pale pink animals familiar from photographs are mostly the product of captive breeding. Under certain unusual conditions, axolotls can be induced to transform into a land-dwelling form, but in nature this almost never happens. B In the wild, axolotls are found only in a small area near Mexico City, in the remains of an ancient lake system. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, was built on an island in one of these lakes, and the Aztecs created floating fields called chinampas, artificial islands of mud and plant material separated by canals, to grow crops. The axolotl was a familiar part of this world. It was eaten as food, used in medicine and associated with the god Xolotl, from whom its name is thought to derive. Axolotls were sold in the markets of the city for centuries, and they remained a local delicacy long after the Spanish conquest. C Today, the axolotl is critically endangered in the wild. Most of the lakes have been drained as Mexico City has expanded, and the remaining canals of Xochimilco suffer from pollution and from the introduction of non-native fish such as carp and tilapia, which compete with axolotls for food and eat their eggs and young. Surveys carried out by researchers suggest that the density of axolotls in the canals has fallen dramatically since the late 1990s, and some scientists fear that the species could disappear from the wild altogether. Why We Put Things Off Almost everyone procrastinates sometimes. We delay writing the difficult email, leave the tax form until the night before it is due, or tidy a drawer instead of starting an important report. For a minority of people, procrastination is a serious and persistent problem that damages their work, their finances and their health. The usual explanation is that procrastinators are lazy or badly organised. I want to argue that this explanation is mostly wrong, and that recognising why is the first step towards doing something about it. Laziness implies an unwillingness to make an effort. Yet procrastinators are often extremely busy. The student who has not started her essay may have spent the afternoon cleaning the kitchen, answering messages and reorganising her notes. What she has avoided is not effort but one particular task, and the reason, according to a growing body of research, is usually emotional. The task makes her feel anxious, bored, inadequate or uncertain, and putting it off brings immediate relief from that feeling. Procrastination, on this view, is less a problem of time management than a problem of managing emotions. This also explains why the tasks we put off are so often the ones that matter most to us: the more important a task is, the more anxiety it can provoke. This explains why the habit is so hard to break. Every time we put off an unpleasant task, we are rewarded with a moment of relief, and behaviour that is rewarded tends to be repeated. The cost, meanwhile, falls on our future selves, who must deal with the same task under greater pressure. Psychologists have found that many people think about their future selves almost as if they were strangers, which may make it easier to pass problems on to them. We imagine that tomorrow we will feel more energetic and confident, although experience should tell us otherwise. If procrastination is driven by emotion, then some common remedies are likely to fail. Telling a procrastinator to try harder, or to make a more detailed timetable, does nothing to address the feelings that cause the delay, and may even make matters worse by adding guilt to the existing anxiety. Harsh self-criticism has a similar effect. In one study of university students, those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before a first examination procrastinated less when preparing for the next one. Being kind to oneself, it seems, is not an excuse for avoiding work but a way of making it easier to begin. There are also practical strategies that work with our emotions rather than against them. One is to make the first step so small that it provokes little anxiety: not writing the report, but opening the document and typing a heading. Starting is usually the hardest part, and once we have begun, the task often seems less threatening. Many people find that they continue well beyond the small step they had planned. Another is to decide in advance exactly when and where we will do something, using a simple plan of the form 'when it is nine o'clock tomorrow, I will sit at my desk and make the phone call'. Research suggests that such specific plans make it considerably more likely that people will follow through. I do not want to suggest that all delay is harmful. Sometimes putting off a decision allows us to gather more information, and some people claim that they do their best work under the pressure of a deadline. But there is a difference between deliberately choosing to wait and repeatedly avoiding a task while feeling bad about it. It is the second pattern that deserves our attention, because it is the one that causes stress, wastes time and, in its more serious forms, can damage careers and relationships. Our culture offers countless productivity tools and techniques, from apps to elaborate filing systems. Many of them are useful, but they rest on the assumption that the procrastinator simply lacks a good system. For most of us, the problem lies elsewhere. Understanding the feelings that lie behind our delays, and responding to them with patience rather than contempt, may achieve more than any timetable or app, however cleverly it has been designed. Why We Put Things Off Almost everyone procrastinates sometimes. We delay writing the difficult email, leave the tax form until the night before it is due, or tidy a drawer instead of starting an important report. For a minority of people, procrastination is a serious and persistent problem that damages their work, their finances and their health. The usual explanation is that procrastinators are lazy or badly organised. I want to argue that this explanation is mostly wrong, and that recognising why is the first step towards doing something about it. Laziness implies an unwillingness to make an effort. Yet procrastinators are often extremely busy. The student who has not started her essay may have spent the afternoon cleaning the kitchen, answering messages and reorganising her notes. What she has avoided is not effort but one particular task, and the reason, according to a growing body of research, is usually emotional. The task makes her feel anxious, bored, inadequate or uncertain, and putting it off brings immediate relief from that feeling. Procrastination, on this view, is less a problem of time management than a problem of managing emotions. This also explains why the tasks we put off are so often the ones that matter most to us: the more important a task is, the more anxiety it can provoke. This explains why the habit is so hard to break. Every time we put off an unpleasant task, we are rewarded with a moment of relief, and behaviour that is rewarded tends to be repeated. The cost, meanwhile, falls on our future selves, who must deal with the same task under greater pressure. Psychologists have found that many people think about their future selves almost as if they were strangers, which may make it easier to pass problems on to them. We imagine that tomorrow we will feel more energetic and confident, although experience should tell us otherwise. If procrastination is driven by emotion, then some common remedies are likely to fail. Telling a procrastinator to try harder, or to make a more detailed timetable, does nothing to address the feelings that cause the delay, and may even make matters worse by adding guilt to the existing anxiety. Harsh self-criticism has a similar effect. In one study of university students, those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before a first examination procrastinated less when preparing for the next one. Being kind to oneself, it seems, is not an excuse for avoiding work but a way of making it easier to begin. There are also practical strategies that work with our emotions rather than against them. One is to make the first step so small that it provokes little anxiety: not writing the report, but opening the document and typing a heading. Starting is usually the hardest part, and once we have begun, the task often seems less threatening. Many people find that they continue well beyond the small step they had planned. Another is to decide in advance exactly when and where we will do something, using a simple plan of the form 'when it is nine o'clock tomorrow, I will sit at my desk and make the phone call'. Research suggests that such specific plans make it considerably more likely that people will follow through. I do not want to suggest that all delay is harmful. options.en: Buy something to eat Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Spread of Paper For centuries, writers in ancient China recorded texts on strips of bamboo tied together with cord, or on silk. Bamboo was cheap but heavy and bulky: a single long work could fill a cart. Silk was light and smooth but far too expensive for everyday use. According to tradition, a court official named Cai Lun invented paper in 105 CE by pounding tree bark, hemp, old rags, and fishing nets into a pulp, spreading it thin, and letting it dry. Archaeologists, however, have found fragments of paper that are considerably older than Cai Lun's time. Most historians now believe that Cai Lun refined an existing technique and promoted it at court, making paper more practical to produce. Over the following centuries, papermaking spread across East Asia. It reached the Islamic world in the eighth century; one well-known account links its arrival in the city of Samarkand to Chinese papermakers captured after a battle in 751. It reached the Islamic world in the eighth century; one well-known account links its arrival in the city of Samarkand to Chinese papermakers captured after a battle in 751. The Dust Bowl During the 1930s, a series of severe droughts struck the southern Great Plains of the United States. Without rain, crops failed, and strong winds lifted the dry topsoil into enormous dust storms. Some storms, known as 'black blizzards', darkened the sky at midday and carried dust hundreds of kilometers to the east. The droughts alone did not cause the disaster. In the preceding decades, high wheat prices and new machinery such as tractors had encouraged farmers to plow millions of acres of native prairie grass. Those grasses had deep roots that held the soil in place and retained moisture. Once they were removed, the exposed soil was easily blown away, and the drought exacerbated a problem that farming practices had created. The federal government responded with new programs. In 1935, it established the Soil Conservation Service, which taught farmers techniques such as contour plowing, crop rotation, and planting rows of trees as windbreaks. These methods reduced erosion significantly, and when rain finally returned in the late 1930s, the region gradually recovered, though many families had already left in search of work elsewhere.

options.en: Call the airport for information Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Seeing with Sound Most bats hunt at night, when their eyes are of limited use. Instead, many species rely on echolocation. A bat produces a series of very high-pitched calls, usually far above the range of human hearing, and listens for the echoes that bounce back from objects around it. By comparing the timing and strength of these echoes, the bat builds a detailed picture of its surroundings. Echolocation is remarkably precise. Some bats can detect a wire thinner than a human hair, and many can judge not only the distance to an insect but also its size and the direction in which it is moving. As a bat closes in on its prey, it calls more and more rapidly, producing a final 'buzz' of up to two hundred calls per second just before the catch. Insects have not been passive victims. Some moths have evolved ears that are sensitive to bat calls; when they hear one, they fold their wings and drop toward the ground. Others produce clicking sounds of their own, which may warn bats that they taste unpleasant or interfere with the bats' ability to process echoes.

The Coffeehouses of London Coffee arrived in England in the mid-seventeenth century, and the first London coffeehouse opened in 1652. Within a few decades, the city had hundreds of them. For the price of a single cup, customers could stay for hours, reading newspapers and joining conversations with strangers. Coffeehouses quickly became centers of information. Newspapers and pamphlets were left on the tables, and news from ships and foreign cities often reached coffeehouses before it reached anyone else. Because people of different social ranks sat at the same tables, the coffeehouses were sometimes called 'penny universities': for the cost of a penny, anyone could listen to discussions of politics, science, and trade. Some coffeehouses became associated with particular activities. Merchants and ship owners gathered at Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse to exchange shipping news, and this gathering eventually developed into Lloyd's of London, one of the world's best-known insurance markets. Not everyone approved of these lively spaces, however. In 1675, King Charles II tried to close them, fearing that they encouraged criticism of the government. The order caused such protest that it was withdrawn within days.

The Monarch Migration Each autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave the northern United States and southern Canada and fly south, some traveling more than 4,000 kilometers. Most of the eastern population spends the winter in a small area of mountain forest in central Mexico, where the butterflies cluster so densely on fir trees that branches bend under their weight. What makes this journey remarkable is that no individual butterfly makes the round trip. The monarchs that fly south in autumn live for up to eight months, far longer than summer generations, which live only a few weeks. In spring, they begin flying north and lay eggs along the way. It takes three or four generations to reach the northern breeding grounds, so the butterflies that arrive in Mexico the following autumn have never been there before. Researchers have found that monarchs navigate partly by using the position of the sun, combined with an internal clock located in their antennae. Experiments suggest that they may also sense Earth's magnetic field, which could help them on cloudy days. How they find the same few mountain forests each year, however, remains uncertain.

Most of the eastern population spends the winter in a small area of mountain forest in central Mexico, where the butterflies cluster so densely on fir trees that branches bend under their weight. What makes this journey remarkable is that no individual butterfly makes the round trip. The monarchs that fly south in autumn live for up to eight months, far longer than summer generations, which live only a few weeks. In spring, they begin flying north and lay eggs along the way. It takes three or four generations to reach the northern breeding grounds, so the butterflies that arrive in Mexico the following autumn have never been there before. Researchers have found that monarchs navigate partly by using the position of the sun, combined with an internal clock located in their antennae. Experiments suggest that they may also sense Earth's magnetic field, which could help them on cloudy days. How they find the same few mountain forests each year, however, remains uncertain.

The Inca Road System At its height in the early sixteenth century, the Inca Empire stretched more than 4,000 kilometers along the western side of South America. Holding together such a vast territory, much of it in the high Andes mountains, required an extraordinary network of roads. The Inca road system, known as the Qhapaq Nan, eventually covered roughly 40,000 kilometers. The Inca did not use wheeled vehicles or horses, so their roads were designed for people on foot and for herds of llamas carrying goods. Where the terrain was steep, builders cut stone staircases into the mountainside. To cross deep river gorges, communities wove suspension bridges from grass rope, which had to be rebuilt regularly. One such bridge, at Q'eswachaka in Peru, is still rebuilt by local villagers every year. Along the roads, the state built thousands of way stations where travelers could rest and find supplies. Messengers called chasquis ran in relays between the stations, passing spoken messages and knotted cords called khipus from one runner to the next. Using this system, news could travel hundreds of kilometers in a single day.

The Value of Salt Today salt is one of the cheapest items in any grocery store, but for most of human history it was a valuable commodity. Humans and their animals need salt to survive, and before refrigeration, salt was also the most important way to preserve food. Meat and fish packed in salt could be stored for months and transported over long distances. Because salt was so essential, its production and trade were often controlled by governments. In ancient China, the state held a monopoly on salt for long periods, and salt taxes provided a large share of government income. In parts of West Africa, salt from the Sahara was carried south by camel caravans and was sometimes traded for gold. Salt has also left its mark on language. The English word 'salary' is often said to come from a Roman practice of paying soldiers in salt, although historians point out that there is little direct evidence for this story. What is certain is that the Latin word for salt, sal, is the origin of words such as 'salad', from the Roman habit of salting vegetables.

Tsunamis A tsunami is a series of ocean waves caused by a sudden, large movement of water, most often an undersea earthquake. When part of the sea floor suddenly rises or drops, the entire column of water above it moves, and waves spread outward in all directions. In the deep ocean, a tsunami may be less than a meter high and can pass beneath a ship almost unnoticed. However, it travels at tremendous speed, sometimes more than 700 kilometers per hour, about as fast as a jet airplane. As the waves approach the shore and the water becomes shallower, they slow down, and their energy is compressed into a much smaller volume of water. As a result, they grow dramatically in height. One of the warning signs of an approaching tsunami is a sudden retreat of the sea, which can expose large areas of the sea floor. Some people have been drawn out to look, not realizing the danger. Today, networks of sensors on the ocean floor detect changes in water pressure and send alerts, giving coastal communities time to move to higher ground.

The Origins of Writing Writing was invented independently in several parts of the world, but the earliest known system developed in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, more than five thousand years ago. Surprisingly, it was not created to record stories or laws. The first written records were accounts: lists of goods such as grain, sheep, and beer that were collected, stored, and distributed by temple officials. These early records used simple pictures pressed into tablets of wet clay. Over time, scribes began making the signs with the cut end of a reed, which left wedge-shaped marks. This style of writing is known as cuneiform, from the Latin word for 'wedge'. The pictures gradually became more abstract, and scribes began to use some signs for their sounds rather than their meanings, which allowed them to write names and, eventually, complete sentences. Once writing could represent spoken language, its uses multiplied. Cuneiform was used for letters, contracts, laws, and literature, including one of the oldest surviving epic poems. Learning it, however, took years of training, and only a small group of professional scribes could read and write. The system remained in use for about three thousand years before it was gradually replaced by alphabets, which needed far fewer signs.

options.en: The student should take yoga first. Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Ocean Currents and Climate The oceans are constantly moving. At the surface, winds push the water into great currents that flow for thousands of kilometers. One of the best known is the Gulf Stream, which carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico northward along the coast of North America and then across the Atlantic toward Europe. Along the way, it releases heat into the atmosphere. This heat helps explain why parts of northwestern Europe have relatively mild winters. Places in Britain and Norway, for example, are generally much warmer in winter than places at similar latitudes in eastern Canada, although scientists point out that winds and the shape of the continents also contribute to the difference. Deep below the surface, currents are driven not by wind but by differences in temperature and saltiness. In the far North Atlantic, surface water becomes very cold and salty, which makes it dense, so it sinks and flows slowly southward along the ocean floor. Water moving through this global system may take around a thousand years to complete a full circuit. Some scientists are concerned that melting ice could add so much fresh water to the North Atlantic that the sinking slows, which could change weather patterns on both sides of the ocean.

options.en: His laptop Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Flattening the Globe: The Mercator Projection Any flat map of the world is a compromise. Earth is round, and it is impossible to flatten the surface of a sphere without stretching or tearing it somewhere. Mapmakers use mathematical methods called projections to transfer the globe onto paper, and every projection distorts something: shapes, sizes, distances, or directions. One of the most famous projections was published in 1569 by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator. His map was designed for sailors. On it, a line of constant compass direction appears as a straight line, so a navigator could draw a course between two ports with a ruler and follow a single compass bearing. To achieve this, Mercator had to stretch the map more and more toward the poles. The result is that areas far from the equator appear much larger than they really are. Greenland, for example, looks about as large as Africa on a Mercator map, although Africa is roughly fourteen times bigger. Because the projection was used for centuries on classroom walls, critics argue that it has given many people a distorted picture of the world. Today, many atlases use other projections for general maps, though Mercator's design is still used for navigation and for many online street maps.

The Towns of Prairie Dogs Prairie dogs are not dogs at all but burrowing rodents related to squirrels. They live on the grasslands of western North America in large colonies known as towns. Some towns once covered hundreds of square kilometers and contained millions of animals. Each town is divided into small family groups called coteries, which defend their own section of the burrow system. Prairie dogs have a complex system of alarm calls. Researchers who recorded these calls found that they vary depending on the type of predator. A call warning of a hawk, for example, sounds different from one warning of a coyote, and the animals respond differently: they dive into their burrows when a hawk is announced but stand upright and watch when a coyote approaches. Some studies suggest that the calls even contain information about a predator's size and color. Prairie dogs are also important to the grassland ecosystem. Their digging mixes and loosens the soil, and their constant grazing keeps grass short, which encourages new growth that bison and other grazers prefer. Their burrows provide shelter for burrowing owls, snakes, and insects, and the prairie dogs themselves are food for many predators. Because so many species depend on them, ecologists describe prairie dogs as a keystone species. Yet their numbers have fallen dramatically over the past century, largely because of farming and disease.

D) The Green route goes downtown. Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Towns of Prairie Dogs Prairie dogs are not dogs at all but burrowing rodents related to squirrels. They live on the grasslands of western North America in large colonies known as towns. Some towns once covered hundreds of square kilometers and contained millions of animals. Each town is divided into small family groups called coteries, which defend their own section of the burrow system. Prairie dogs have a complex system of alarm calls. Researchers who recorded these calls found that they vary depending on the type of predator. A call warning of a hawk, for example, sounds different from one warning of a coyote, and the animals respond differently: they dive into their burrows when a hawk is announced but stand upright and watch when a coyote approaches. Some studies suggest that the calls even contain information about a predator's size and color. Prairie dogs are also important to the grassland ecosystem. Their digging mixes and loosens the soil, and their constant grazing keeps grass short, which encourages new growth that bison and other grazers prefer. Their burrows provide shelter for burrowing owls, snakes, and insects, and the prairie dogs themselves are food for many predators. Because so many species depend on them, ecologists describe prairie dogs as a keystone species. Yet their numbers have fallen dramatically over the past century, largely because of farming and disease. According to paragraph 1, what is a coterie?

The Harlem Renaissance In the early twentieth century, hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the rural South to cities in the North, a movement known as the Great Migration. Many settled in Harlem, a neighborhood in New York City. By the 1920s, Harlem had become the center of a remarkable burst of creativity in literature, music, and art that later became known as the Harlem Renaissance. Writers of the movement explored Black identity and everyday life with new pride and honesty. The poet Langston Hughes wrote about ordinary working people and used the rhythms of blues and jazz in his poems. In 1925, the philosopher Alain Locke published an influential collection of writing called The New Negro, which argued that Black artists could change how the nation saw African Americans. At the same time, jazz musicians such as Duke Ellington performed in Harlem's famous clubs, attracting large audiences. The Great Depression, which began in 1929, brought hard times to Harlem, and by the mid-1930s the movement had faded. Its influence, however, lasted much longer. The writers and musicians of the Harlem Renaissance inspired later generations of artists and helped prepare the ground for the civil rights movement.

options.en: It must submit a printed copy. Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Paintings of Lascaux In 1940, four teenagers exploring a hillside in southwestern France found a narrow opening that led into a cave. Inside, they discovered walls covered with paintings of animals. The cave, called Lascaux, contains around six hundred paintings and about fifteen hundred engravings, and scientists estimate that they were made roughly seventeen thousand years ago. The most common subjects are horses, but the walls also show deer, bison, and large wild cattle called aurochs. The artists made their paints from minerals: red and yellow came from iron-rich earth, and black came from manganese and charcoal. They applied the paint with brushes, pads of moss or fur, and possibly by blowing it through hollow bones. Many of the images were painted high on the walls and ceilings, which suggests that the artists built some kind of scaffolding to reach them. After the cave opened to the public in 1948, more than a thousand visitors a day came to see it. Unfortunately, the carbon dioxide and moisture from their breath began to damage the paintings, and green growths appeared on the walls. In 1963, the cave was closed to the public. Twenty years later, an exact copy of part of the cave, called Lascaux II, was opened nearby so that visitors could still experience the art without harming the original.
