The Story of the Ukulele The ukulele is a small, four-stringed instrument closely associated with Hawaii, but its origins lie thousands of kilometers away. In 1879, a ship arrived in Honolulu carrying hundreds of workers from the Portuguese island of Madeira, who had come to work on Hawaii's sugar plantations. Among them were several skilled woodworkers who brought with them a small guitar-like instrument called the machete. Soon after arriving, these craftsmen opened shops in Honolulu and began making instruments for local customers. Hawaiians quickly adopted the instrument and changed it to suit their own music. Makers began using koa, a wood that grows only in Hawaii and produces a warm, bright sound. The new instrument was named the ukulele, a Hawaiian word that is often translated as 'jumping flea,' perhaps because of the quick movement of a player's fingers. King Kalakaua, who ruled Hawaii at the time, was an enthusiastic supporter of traditional music and dance, and he featured the ukulele at royal events, which greatly increased its popularity. The ukulele became famous in the mainland United States after 1915, when Hawaiian musicians performed at a large international exhibition in San Francisco. Millions of visitors heard the instrument for the first time, and sales soared. Because ukuleles were inexpensive and relatively easy to learn, they became popular with amateur musicians. After a period of decline, the instrument has enjoyed a strong revival in recent decades, partly thanks to online videos in which performers share songs and lessons.

In 1879, a ship arrived in Honolulu carrying hundreds of workers from the Portuguese island of Madeira, who had come to work on Hawaii's sugar plantations. Among them were several skilled woodworkers who brought with them a small guitar-like instrument called the machete. Soon after arriving, these craftsmen opened shops in Honolulu and began making instruments for local customers. Hawaiians quickly adopted the instrument and changed it to suit their own music. Makers began using koa, a wood that grows only in Hawaii and produces a warm, bright sound. The new instrument was named the ukulele, a Hawaiian word that is often translated as 'jumping flea,' perhaps because of the quick movement of a player's fingers. King Kalakaua, who ruled Hawaii at the time, was an enthusiastic supporter of traditional music and dance, and he featured the ukulele at royal events, which greatly increased its popularity. The ukulele became famous in the mainland United States after 1915, when Hawaiian musicians performed at a large international exhibition in San Francisco. Millions of visitors heard the instrument for the first time, and sales soared. Because ukuleles were inexpensive and relatively easy to learn, they became popular with amateur musicians. After a period of decline, the instrument has enjoyed a strong revival in recent decades, partly thanks to online videos in which performers share songs and lessons. According to paragraph 1, who brought the instrument that became the ukulele to Hawaii?

The Rise of Impressionism In nineteenth-century France, the most important place for an artist to show work was the official Salon, a huge annual exhibition in Paris. Its judges preferred carefully finished paintings of historical, religious, or mythological scenes, with smooth surfaces and invisible brushstrokes. Many young painters found these rules restrictive, and in 1863 so many works were rejected that the emperor allowed a separate exhibition for them, which became known as the Salon of the Rejected. In 1874, a group of these independent artists, including Camille Pissarro, Edgar Degas, and Berthe Morisot, organized their own exhibition. One critic mocked a painting in the show titled Impression, Sunrise, calling the whole group 'Impressionists.' The artists adopted the name. Rather than historical scenes, they painted modern life: city streets, cafés, train stations, and people relaxing in the countryside. They often worked outdoors, using quick, visible brushstrokes to capture the changing effects of light. Two inventions helped make this approach possible. Paint sold in metal tubes, available from the 1840s, allowed artists to carry their colors outside easily. New railway lines made it simple to travel from Paris to the coast or the countryside in a few hours. Although the Impressionists were often criticized at first, collectors gradually began buying their work, and by the end of the century their style had influenced painters around the world.

The Mountain Rice Terraces of the Philippines In the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, in the Philippines, steep slopes are covered with thousands of narrow, flat fields that rise like giant staircases. These rice terraces were built by the Ifugao people, and many of them are believed to be several hundred years old. In some places, the terraces climb more than a thousand meters up the mountainsides, and in 1995 a group of them was added to the list of World Heritage Sites. Growing rice on a mountain requires careful control of water. The Ifugao built the terraces with stone or earth walls and leveled each field so that it could hold a shallow pool of water. Water from streams and forests higher up the mountain is guided through a system of channels and bamboo pipes, flowing from one terrace to the next. Because the forests above the fields store rainwater and release it slowly, protecting these woodlands has always been part of farming the terraces. Today the terraces face serious threats. Many young people have moved to cities for work, leaving fewer farmers to repair walls and clear channels. When a wall collapses and is not repaired, water escapes and nearby fields can be damaged as well. Local organizations now run programs that teach traditional building methods to students and that encourage tourists to visit, hoping that new income will give young people a reason to stay.

options.en: He must pay the full team fee. Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Dunning-Kruger Effect In 1999, the psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger published a study with a surprising finding. They gave university students tests of logical reasoning, grammar, and humor, and then asked each student to estimate how well they had done compared with others. Students who scored in the bottom quarter believed, on average, that they had performed better than most of their classmates. Their estimates were far higher than their actual results. Dunning and Kruger offered an explanation for this pattern. The skills needed to perform well in an area are often the same skills needed to judge performance in that area. A person who does not know the rules of grammar, for example, cannot easily recognize the mistakes in his own writing. In other words, people with little skill suffer twice: they make errors, and they are unable to see that they are making them. The researchers also found that the problem could be reduced. When low-scoring students were given a short lesson in the skill being tested, they became much better at judging their earlier performance and lowered their estimates. Interestingly, the highest-scoring students showed the opposite tendency: they slightly underestimated how well they had done, apparently because they assumed that tasks easy for them were also easy for everyone else.

The Way of Tea Tea arrived in Japan from China more than a thousand years ago, first as a medicine and later as a drink enjoyed by Buddhist monks, who used it to stay awake during long hours of meditation. Over several centuries, preparing and serving tea developed into a formal ceremony known as chanoyu, which means 'hot water for tea.' The ceremony uses matcha, a fine green powder that is whisked with hot water in a bowl rather than steeped in a pot. The tea master most responsible for shaping the ceremony was Sen no Rikyu, who lived in the sixteenth century. Rikyu rejected the fashion among wealthy lords for displaying expensive Chinese tea bowls and elaborate decorations. Instead, he favored simple, rough pottery and small, plain tea rooms, some with an entrance so low that guests had to bow and crawl inside. This, he believed, reminded everyone, whatever their rank, that they were equal inside the tea room. Every movement in the ceremony follows a set pattern, from the way the host cleans each utensil to the way guests turn the bowl before drinking. To an outsider, these rules may seem strict, but practitioners say they free the mind from everyday concerns and allow host and guests to focus completely on the present moment. Today, many Japanese people study the tea ceremony for years, and schools founded by Rikyu's descendants still teach it.

Glassblowing in the Roman World People in Mesopotamia and Egypt were making glass objects more than three thousand years ago, but for most of that time glass was rare and expensive. Craftsmen shaped it by pouring melted glass into molds or by winding hot threads of glass around a core of clay. These slow methods produced small, colorful beads and bottles that only the wealthy could afford. Around the first century BCE, craftsmen on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean discovered that they could blow air through a hollow metal tube into a blob of melted glass, inflating it like a bubble. This technique, glassblowing, allowed a skilled worker to make a cup or bottle in minutes rather than hours. The new method spread quickly across the Roman Empire, and workshops appeared in Italy, Gaul, and along the Rhine. As production became faster and cheaper, glass entered ordinary Roman homes. Families used glass jars to store food and wine, and because glass could be clear, people could see what was inside without opening the container. Wealthy Romans even began to fit small panes of glass into windows. Archaeologists find fragments of Roman glass at sites across Europe, evidence of how widely the new technology was adopted.

The Invention of the Stethoscope Before the nineteenth century, a doctor who wanted to listen to a patient's heart or lungs had only one option: to press an ear directly against the patient's chest. This method, known as immediate auscultation, was often uncomfortable for doctor and patient alike, and it worked poorly when the patient was large or was wearing thick clothing. In 1816, the French physician René Laennec faced exactly this problem while examining a young woman with heart trouble. He remembered watching children send sounds along a wooden beam by scratching one end of it, so he rolled several sheets of paper into a tight tube, placed one end on the patient's chest, and listened at the other. To his surprise, the heartbeat sounded clearer than it ever had through his bare ear. The Northern Lights For thousands of years, people living in the far north have watched curtains of green and red light ripple across the night sky. These displays are called auroras: the aurora borealis in the Northern Hemisphere and the aurora australis in the Southern Hemisphere. Although they can resemble clouds lit from below, auroras mostly occur between about 100 and 300 kilometers above the ground, far higher than any weather. Their ultimate source is the Sun. Besides light and heat, the Sun constantly releases a stream of electrically charged particles known as the solar wind. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of these particles, but it also guides some of their energy toward the regions around the magnetic poles. There, charged particles collide with atoms and molecules in the upper atmosphere, giving them extra energy that they then release as light, somewhat as the gas inside a neon sign glows when electricity passes through it. The color depends on which gas is struck and at what height. Oxygen between roughly 100 and 200 kilometers produces the most common color, a yellowish green, whereas oxygen higher up, where the air is extremely thin, gives off a rarer deep red. Nitrogen adds touches of blue and purple, usually along the lower edges. During strong solar storms, the zone of activity expands toward the equator, which is why auroras are occasionally seen far from the poles.

options.en: Wait in the atrium Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Why Onions Make Us Cry Almost everyone who cooks has experienced it: you begin chopping an onion, and within seconds your eyes start to sting and fill with tears. For a long time, people assumed that onion juice simply splashed into the eyes, but the real cause is a chemical reaction that the onion sets off to defend itself. An intact onion stores sulfur-containing compounds and certain enzymes in separate compartments of its cells. When a knife breaks those cells open, the compounds and enzymes mix. In a rapid chain of reactions, they produce a volatile compound called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. Because the compound turns into vapor easily, it drifts upward from the cutting board and reaches the eyes, where it stimulates nerves that signal the tear glands to wash the irritant away. Scientists believe this reaction evolved to discourage animals from eating onion bulbs. Cooks, meanwhile, have developed their own defenses. Chilling an onion before cutting it slows the reaction, and a very sharp knife crushes fewer cells than a dull one. Researchers in Japan have even bred an onion that produces almost none of the irritating compound, although it has not replaced ordinary onions in most kitchens.

options.en: Group tickets are not available. Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Living Light in the Deep Sea In the ocean, sunlight fades quickly with depth: a few hundred meters down only a faint blue glow remains, and below about a thousand meters there is none at all. In that deep darkness, the only light comes from living things. A remarkable number of deep-sea animals, including fish, squid, shrimp, and jellies, can produce their own light, a process called bioluminescence. In one survey of animals filmed off the coast of California, roughly three-quarters of the creatures observed were able to glow. The light is produced by a chemical reaction in which a compound generally known as luciferin combines with oxygen, assisted by an enzyme called luciferase. Almost all of the energy is released as light rather than heat, which is why bioluminescence is sometimes described as 'cold light.' Most deep-sea species glow blue or blue-green, the colors that travel farthest through seawater. Animals use this ability in strikingly different ways. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth to attract prey. Some shrimp, when attacked, release a cloud of luminous fluid that may distract a predator long enough for the shrimp to escape. Perhaps most ingenious is counterillumination: in the dim upper layer where some sunlight still reaches, hatchetfish produce a faint glow along their bellies that matches the dim light filtering down from above, making their outlines almost invisible to predators looking up from below.

options.en: In her own room Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. How Cats Came to Live with People Unlike dogs, which humans appear to have deliberately bred for tasks such as hunting and guarding, cats may have largely domesticated themselves. Genetic studies indicate that today's house cats are descended from a wildcat of North Africa and Southwest Asia. The process probably began about ten thousand years ago in the Fertile Crescent, when people first started farming and storing grain. Stored grain attracted mice and rats, and the rodents in turn attracted wildcats. Cats that were less fearful of humans could hunt around the villages and enjoy a reliable food supply. Farmers, for their part, had good reason to tolerate animals that protected their harvests. Over many generations, the tamer cats spread along with human communities. Some of the earliest evidence of a close bond comes from Cyprus, where archaeologists found a cat buried beside a person in a grave about 9,500 years old. Because wildcats are not native to the island, people must have brought them there by boat. Much later, the ancient Egyptians kept cats in large numbers and portrayed them in art, and cats then spread along trade routes across the Mediterranean and beyond.

options.en: Seniors Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. How Cacti Survive in the Desert Cacti thrive in some of the driest places on Earth, where rain may fall only a few times a year. Their success depends on a combination of features that allow them to collect water quickly, store it for long periods, and lose as little of it as possible. Most cacti have shallow but extremely wide root systems that spread just below the surface. When rain does fall, these roots can absorb large amounts of water before it evaporates, and some species grow new fine roots within hours of a shower. The water is stored in the thick stem, whose folds, or pleats, allow it to expand like an accordion as it fills and to shrink again during a drought. Equally important is how cacti limit water loss. Their leaves have been reduced to spines, which shade the stem and trap a thin layer of still air around it. In addition, many cacti use a special form of photosynthesis. Ordinary plants open the tiny pores on their surfaces during the day to take in carbon dioxide, losing water in the process. Cacti instead open their pores at night, when the air is cooler and more humid, store the carbon dioxide chemically, and use it for photosynthesis the following day while their pores stay closed.

The Pony Express In 1860, a letter sent from the eastern United States to California could take weeks to arrive by ship or stagecoach. That April, a private company launched the Pony Express, a relay system of riders on horseback that carried mail between St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, a distance of roughly 3,000 kilometers, in about ten days. The system depended on speed above all else. Riders were usually young and light, and they carried mail in a leather cover that could be moved from one saddle to another in seconds. Every 15 to 25 kilometers, they reached a station where a fresh horse was waiting, and each rider typically covered more than 100 kilometers before handing the mail to the next. Despite its fame, the Pony Express lasted only about eighteen months. In October 1861, the first telegraph line across the continent was completed, allowing messages to cross the country in minutes. The company, which had never made a profit, closed two days later. Yet the riders' daring journeys captured the public imagination, and the Pony Express remains one of the best-known symbols of the American West.

Mimicry in Nature Many animals protect themselves from predators by being poisonous, foul-tasting, or able to sting, and they often advertise this with bold colors such as yellow, black, or red. A predator that attacks one of these animals and has an unpleasant experience quickly learns to avoid anything that looks similar. This learning has opened the door to an evolutionary strategy known as mimicry. In Batesian mimicry, named after the nineteenth-century naturalist Henry Walter Bates, a harmless species evolves to resemble a dangerous one. Many hoverflies, for example, have yellow and black stripes that make them look like wasps, although they cannot sting. Birds that have learned to avoid wasps tend to leave the hoverflies alone as well. This arrangement works only as long as the mimics remain relatively rare; if harmless lookalikes became too common, predators would more often discover that the warning colors meant nothing. A second form, Müllerian mimicry, involves two or more species that are all genuinely harmful and have come to look alike. In this case, every species benefits: because predators learn a shared pattern faster, fewer individuals of each species are killed while predators are learning. Several species of tropical Heliconius butterflies, all of which taste bad to birds, share nearly identical wing patterns for this reason.

The Collapse of the Grand Banks Cod For nearly five hundred years, the Grand Banks, an area of shallow ocean off the coast of Newfoundland in eastern Canada, supported one of the richest fisheries in the world. Explorers in the late 1400s reported that cod were so plentiful there that they could be scooped out of the water in baskets. For centuries, fishermen in small boats caught them with hooks and lines, and the cod population remained large. This changed after the 1950s, when huge factory trawlers from many countries began working the area. These ships dragged enormous nets along the sea floor and could freeze and process their catch on board, which allowed them to stay at sea for weeks. The total catch rose sharply, peaking in the late 1960s at roughly 800,000 tonnes in a single year. Because the trawlers caught so many young fish before they were old enough to breed, the population could not replace itself. Scientists' estimates of the stock were too optimistic, and catch limits remained high even as fishermen found it harder and harder to fill their boats. By 1992, the cod had almost disappeared, and the Canadian government banned fishing for northern cod. The ban put about 30,000 people out of work, many of them in small coastal towns that had depended on fishing for generations. Although it was expected to last only two years, the cod recovered far more slowly than predicted, and the fishery has never returned to its former size.

options.en: 9 a.m. on Saturday Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. An Echo of the Big Bang In 1964, two radio astronomers at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, were troubled by a faint hiss in their large horn-shaped antenna. The signal was the same no matter which direction they pointed the antenna, and it did not change with the time of day or the season. Suspecting a fault in their equipment, they even removed pigeons that had been nesting inside the antenna and cleaned out their droppings. The hiss remained. Meanwhile, physicists at nearby Princeton University had predicted that if the universe began in a hot, dense state, as the Big Bang theory proposed, some radiation from that early period should still fill space today. Over billions of years, the expansion of the universe would have stretched this radiation into microwaves, corresponding to a temperature only about three degrees above absolute zero. When the two groups compared notes, they realized that Penzias and Wilson had detected exactly this radiation, now called the cosmic microwave background. The discovery was a turning point. A rival model, the steady-state theory, held that the universe had no beginning and had always looked roughly the same, and it offered no natural explanation for such an even glow coming from every direction. Most astronomers therefore came to accept the Big Bang theory, and in 1978 Penzias and Wilson shared the Nobel Prize in Physics.

options.en: Because the box office closes at 7 Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Safety Elevator Hoists for lifting goods had existed for centuries, but before the 1850s few people were willing to ride in them. The platforms hung from ropes, and if a rope snapped, everything on the platform fell to the bottom of the shaft. As a result, most buildings were limited to five or six stories, the number of flights of stairs that people were willing to climb. In 1852, an American mechanic named Elisha Otis designed a safety device for a hoist in a bed factory. The platform ran between two vertical guide rails lined with teeth. A strong spring was attached to the lifting rope, and as long as the rope was pulling, the spring stayed bent. If the rope broke, the spring straightened instantly, pushing metal arms into the teeth of the rails and locking the platform in place. Otis demonstrated his invention dramatically at an 1854 exhibition in New York. Standing on a raised platform, he ordered the only rope holding it to be cut; the platform dropped a few centimeters and stopped. In 1857, the first passenger elevator using his brake was installed in a New York department store. Safe elevators, together with new steel frames, eventually made the tall office buildings of modern cities possible.

options.en: Only students with a meal plan Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Venus: Earth's Strange Twin Venus is often called Earth's twin. The two planets are nearly the same size and mass, and they formed in the same region of the young solar system from similar materials. Yet conditions on their surfaces could hardly be more different. Venus is wrapped in a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide, with clouds of sulfuric acid. At the surface, the air pressure is about ninety times that on Earth, and the temperature is around 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Venus is in fact hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is much closer to the Sun. The reason is a runaway greenhouse effect: sunlight that reaches the surface warms the ground, but the dense carbon dioxide traps the heat that the ground gives off, so it cannot escape back into space. Many scientists think Venus may once have had oceans. As the young Sun grew brighter, however, the water may have begun to evaporate, and the water vapor, itself a powerful greenhouse gas, would have warmed the planet further, causing even more evaporation. Eventually, sunlight high in the atmosphere broke the water molecules apart, and the light hydrogen escaped into space. Studying how Venus lost its water helps scientists judge which planets around other stars might remain habitable.

prompt.en: 12. Write for an Academic Discussion (10 minutes) Your professor is teaching a class on education. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: • Express and support your opinion. • Make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words. Dr. Solberg: Many schools are considering banning students' smartphones for the whole school day, including during breaks and lunch. options.en: After Sam arrives Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Edward Jenner and the First Vaccine Smallpox was one of the deadliest diseases in human history. In the eighteenth century, it killed hundreds of thousands of people in Europe every year, and many survivors were left with deep scars. People had long noticed that anyone who survived smallpox never caught it again, and some doctors deliberately infected healthy people with material from a mild case. This practice, called variolation, usually produced a less severe illness, but it was risky: some patients died, and others spread the disease. In the 1790s, the English doctor Edward Jenner investigated a belief common among farmers: that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cows, did not get smallpox. In 1796, Jenner took material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and scratched it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy. Weeks later, he exposed the boy to smallpox, and the boy did not become ill. Jenner called his method vaccination, from the Latin word for cow. Because cowpox was far milder than smallpox and did not spread easily between people, vaccination was much safer than variolation, and it was adopted rapidly around the world. Jenner did not know why it worked; the science of the immune system came much later. Nevertheless, his work led, almost two centuries later, to a global campaign that eliminated smallpox. In 1980, the World Health Organization declared the disease eradicated.

options.en: Proof of address Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Bauhaus The Bauhaus was a German school of art and design that operated for only fourteen years, from 1919 to 1933, yet it helped shape the look of the modern world. Its founder, the architect Walter Gropius, wanted to end the traditional separation between fine artists, such as painters, and skilled craftspeople. Students at the Bauhaus learned in workshops, working with wood, metal, textiles, and glass, under the guidance of both an artist and a master craftsman. Bauhaus designers rejected decoration that served no purpose. They believed that the form of an object should follow from its function, and they favored simple geometric shapes, smooth surfaces, and modern materials such as steel tubing and glass. Importantly, they also aimed to design objects that could be produced in factories, so that well-designed furniture and lamps would be affordable for ordinary people rather than only for the wealthy. The school faced constant political pressure. It moved from Weimar to Dessau and finally to Berlin before closing in 1933 under pressure from the Nazi government. Many of its teachers then emigrated, several of them to the United States, where they taught at major universities. Through them, Bauhaus ideas spread widely, and the clean lines of much modern furniture and architecture still reflect the school's influence.

The Dead Sea Scrolls In the winter of 1946–1947, a young shepherd searching for a lost goat in the cliffs near the Dead Sea threw a stone into a cave and heard something break. Inside, he and his cousins found clay jars containing ancient scrolls. Over the next decade, archaeologists and local people searched eleven caves in the area, near a site called Qumran, and recovered the remains of roughly nine hundred manuscripts. The scrolls were written mostly in Hebrew, with others in Aramaic and Greek, and most date from about the third century BCE to the first century CE. Their importance is hard to overstate. About a quarter of them are copies of books from the Hebrew Bible, and they are roughly a thousand years older than the oldest previously known complete manuscripts of those books. Comparing the two showed that, although there were many small differences, the texts had been copied with remarkable care over the centuries. Many of the scrolls survived only as thousands of tiny fragments, and reassembling them has taken scholars decades. In recent years, new technology has helped. Multispectral imaging, which photographs the fragments under different wavelengths of light, can reveal faded writing that is invisible to the eye, and DNA analysis of the animal skins on which many scrolls were written has helped researchers match fragments that belong together.

options.en: Classroom use Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. Reading the Past in Ice In Antarctica and Greenland, snow has fallen year after year for hundreds of thousands of years without melting. As new snow piles up, the older layers below are pressed into solid ice. By drilling deep into these ice sheets and pulling out long cylinders of ice, called ice cores, scientists can read a detailed record of Earth's past climate. The ice preserves several kinds of evidence. Tiny bubbles trapped in the ice contain samples of the ancient atmosphere, so scientists can measure how much carbon dioxide the air held at different times. The chemistry of the ice itself, in particular the ratio of heavier to lighter forms of oxygen in the water molecules, reveals the temperature at the time the snow fell. Layers of ash and dust record volcanic eruptions and dry, windy periods. The oldest continuous ice core, drilled at a site in Antarctica called Dome C, reaches back about 800,000 years. It shows that Earth has repeatedly moved between long ice ages and shorter warm periods, and that temperature and carbon dioxide levels have risen and fallen together throughout that time. It also shows that today's carbon dioxide levels are far higher than at any point in the record, which is one reason ice cores are central to research on climate change.

options.en: Only on the same day Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. The Trade Winds For centuries, sailors crossing the tropical oceans relied on steady winds that blow from the east toward the west. These winds were so dependable that sailors described them as blowing 'trade', an old expression meaning steadily along a fixed path, and they became known as the trade winds. But why do they blow so consistently, and why from the east? The answer begins with the Sun. Near the equator, intense sunlight heats the air, which rises. Cooler air from farther north and south flows toward the equator to replace it. If Earth did not rotate, this air would move straight north or south. However, because Earth spins from west to east, the surface near the equator moves faster than the surface at higher latitudes. Air flowing toward the equator cannot keep up with the faster-moving ground beneath it, so it lags behind and appears to curve toward the west. This apparent deflection is known as the Coriolis effect. As a result, in the Northern Hemisphere the trade winds blow from the northeast, and in the Southern Hemisphere they blow from the southeast. Where the two sets of winds meet, near the equator, the air rises and forms a belt of clouds and heavy rain. Sailors knew this region as the doldrums, because the winds there were often so weak that ships could be stuck for days.

Darwin's Finches When Charles Darwin visited the Galápagos Islands in 1835 during the voyage of HMS Beagle, he collected many small birds. At the time, he did not pay them much attention, and he did not always record which island each bird came from. Only after he returned to England did the bird expert John Gould tell him that the birds, which had very different beaks, were all closely related species of finch. Darwin came to suspect that the finches had descended from a single ancestral species that had arrived from the mainland, and that populations on different islands had adapted to different foods. Species that crush hard seeds have thick, powerful beaks, while those that eat insects have thin, pointed ones. One species even uses cactus spines as tools to pull insects out of holes in trees. More than a century later, the biologists Peter and Rosemary Grant spent decades studying finches on the tiny island of Daphne Major. During a severe drought in 1977, small, soft seeds became scarce, and many finches died. The survivors tended to have larger beaks that could crack the remaining hard seeds, and their offspring inherited those larger beaks. The Grants had observed natural selection taking place within just a few years.

options.en: $18 Read an Academic Passage Read the passage and answer the questions. City Lights and Migrating Birds Every spring and autumn, billions of birds migrate between their breeding grounds and the areas where they spend the winter. Most songbirds migrate at night, when the air is calmer and cooler and there are fewer predators. To find their way, they rely on several cues, including Earth's magnetic field and the positions of the stars. Artificial light at night interferes with this ancient behavior. Brightly lit buildings and towers, especially in fog or low clouds, attract migrating birds and draw them off course. Once they are among the lights, many birds circle repeatedly until they are exhausted, and others crash into glass windows that they cannot see. Researchers estimate that collisions with buildings kill hundreds of millions of birds each year in the United States alone. Fortunately, this problem is easier to solve than many environmental threats. In a number of cities, programs ask the owners of tall buildings to turn off unnecessary lights during the main migration seasons. One study in Chicago found that when fewer windows of a large convention center were lit at night, bird collisions there dropped by more than half. Such programs also save energy, which makes them attractive to building owners.

Dr. Laine: Some popular cities, such as Venice, have started charging tourists a daily fee to enter the city center during busy periods. Supporters say the fees reduce overcrowding and pay for cleaning and repairs. Critics say the fees make travel more expensive and unfairly punish visitors who spend money in local businesses. Should popular tourist cities charge visitors an entry fee? Why or why not? Hiro: Yes. When I visited a famous old town last summer, the streets were so crowded that it wasn't enjoyable at all.
